member.name: T:OpenIGI.Presentation.Cameras.CameraPose
member.summary: A camera as a position and two angles, which is the form every camera in this game actually keeps and the only form that can be interpolated safely.

remarks.para: holds an orientation matrix, and blending two of those directly does not work for anything but a very small angle: the obvious row-by-row lerp leaves a matrix that is no longer a rotation, and re-orthonormalising it does not recover the turn that was meant — which is exactly why documents itself as small-angle only. A cinematic that swings the camera from an orbit to straight down covers about eighty degrees, so it interpolates the angles and rebuilds the matrix instead.

That is sound here because is itself a pure function of a yaw and a pitch, so the round trip through this type is exact up to floating-point error. DeathCamera and InteractionCamera already recover the same pair of angles from a look direction by hand; this is that idiom, named.
The angles are the world's Z-up convention: yaw turns about Z with zero looking along +Y, and pitch is positive looking up.

member.param: The eye, in metres.
The heading in radians; zero looks along +Y.
The elevation in radians; positive looks up.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Presentation.Cameras.CameraPose.FromCamera(OpenIGI.Core.Graphics.Camera3D@)
member.summary: Recovers the pose a camera is in.
member.param: The camera to read.
member.returns: Its position and angles.
member.remarks: The orientation's third row is the view's forward axis in world space, which builds as (sin y cos p, cos y cos p, sin p) — so the pitch comes straight off Z and the yaw off the other two. Clamped before the arc sine because a forward axis that has drifted a hair outside the unit sphere would otherwise come back as NaN and take the whole frame's camera with it.

member.summary: Interpolates between two poses, turning the short way round.
member.param: The pose at = 0.
The pose at = 1.

member.remarks: At = 1 this returns verbatim rather than the arithmetic result. That is not tidiness: from + (to - from) * 1f is not bit-identical to to in floating point, and the whole no-pop guarantee at the end of the mission entry rests on the last cinematic frame being the same camera as the first gameplay frame.

The angle at = 1, in radians.
The blend factor.

member.remarks: Without the wrap a camera at 170 degrees turning to −170 would sweep 340 degrees the wrong way round rather than 20 degrees the right way. folds the difference into [-pi, pi], which is that shorter way.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Presentation.Cameras.FreeCamera
member.summary: A fly-through camera with a scene editor's controls.

remarks.para: A development tool, not a game camera: the original's is a task with a state machine for first-person, third-person, binocular and map views (0x482700, M8). This exists to look at a level that has no player in it yet.

The mapping is the one a Unity scene view uses, and the point of it is that nothing moves the camera unless a mouse button is held — the keyboard alone never does, so a stray key press while looking at something cannot drift the view:

item.description: look around, and W A S D fly while it is held; Q E drop and rise.
pan — the world follows the pointer.
dolly along the view; while right mouse is held it trims the fly speed instead, and the trim sticks.
flat move: fly without changing height.
slower, for placing the view precisely.
turn without the mouse, so a keyboard-only session still works.

remarks.para: Two of the gist's features are not here because they need something the engine does not have yet: double-click to focus wants a collision raycast to pick an object with (M9), and its undo restores only the position that focus moved from.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Presentation.Cameras.HandheldShake
member.summary: The small, slow wander of a camera somebody is holding rather than bolting down.

remarks.para: Two octaves of smoothed value noise per axis, read out of one table drawn at construction. Smoothed rather than linear because linear value noise has a corner at every lattice point, and a camera that changes direction on a corner reads as a mechanism ticking rather than as a person breathing. The second octave is at 2.37 times the first, not twice it: an integer ratio makes both octaves return to phase together on a common period, and the sum acquires an audible beat.

The amplitudes are deliberately tiny — a fifth to a quarter of a degree. This is a long lens on a braced operator, not a chase camera. It is expressed as rotation only, with no positional term, because at the altitude the mission entry holds at, the subject is a hundred metres or more away and an angular disturbance already moves the picture by metres; adding a positional wander would double-count it and would have to be retuned for every altitude, where an angular one is correct at all of them by construction.

It is a pure function of a time and a weight, holds no state between samples, and allocates nothing — so the same second of a sequence looks the same every time it is played, which is what lets a -lockstep capture of the entry be compared frame for frame.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Presentation.Cameras.HandheldShake.Sample(System.Single,System.Single,System.Single@,System.Single@,System.Single@)
member.summary: Samples the wander at a moment.
member.param: How far into the shot this is.
How much of the wander applies, 0 none to 1 all.
Receives the yaw offset in radians.
Receives the pitch offset in radians.
Receives the roll offset in radians.
member.remarks: At a weight of exactly zero every output is exactly zero, which is what lets a shot hand the view over to the player without the last frame differing from the first by a fraction of a degree.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Presentation.Cameras.HandheldShake.ApplyRoll(OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Matrix3f@,System.Single)
member.summary: Rolls an orientation about the direction it is already looking.
member.param: The orientation to roll.
The roll in radians.
member.returns: The rolled orientation.
member.remarks:
cannot express a roll — it is built from a yaw and a pitch alone — but a roll is exactly a rotation about the view's forward axis, and in this convention the orientation's rows are the view axes: right, up, forward. So it mixes the first two rows and leaves the third alone. Six lines, and it is most of the difference between a camera that is shaking and a camera somebody is holding.
A roll of exactly zero returns the orientation unchanged rather than multiplying by an identity built from a cosine and a sine, so a shot that has ramped its shake out ends bit-identical to the pose it was aiming at.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Presentation.Cameras.MapComputerCamera
member.summary: The shot that carries the player out of their own eyes and up into the map, and back down again: a vertical pull-out to the map's vantage, a display being driven from cold, and — when they close it — a fall back into the head from wherever across the level they had panned to.

remarks.para: The deliberate echo of is the point. That shot ends by dropping into the player's eyes; this one begins by reversing it, so opening the computer reads as stepping back out to the vantage the mission was surveyed from. Structured the same way for the same reason: poses and a clock in, a camera and a handful of presentation numbers out, no device and no renderer, so the whole of it can be reasoned about and tested as arithmetic.

The field of view is part of the move. A climb from eye height to the map's altitude is a rise of some nine hundred metres, and covering it at a gameplay field of view is a fall away so fast it reads as a mistake. The map's own view is a long lens — a narrow field from a long way up, which is what makes a map flat — so the shot narrows into it as it climbs, and what the player sees is mostly the perspective flattening rather than the ground receding. That is why is published alongside the camera: the scene pass has to be given both or the move is only half of itself.

The angles resolve early and the height resolves late. The turn to straight down and to north finishes at four fifths of the climb, so the last stretch is a clean vertical rise into a heading that is already correct — a camera still rotating as it arrives reads as a stumble. The descent is the same idea mirrored: it swings out of the map's heading over the first part of the fall and spends the rest of it dropping into a look direction the player is about to be handed.

The close starts where the map is, not where the player is. A player who has panned across the level and closes the computer gets a flight back rather than a cut, which costs nothing to implement — the descent already interpolates from a pose — and is the difference between the map being a screen and the map being a place they were looking at.

member.summary: Interpolates a field of view geometrically rather than linearly.

The angle at = 1, in radians.
The blend factor.

member.remarks: Zoom is perceived in ratios: going from 60 degrees to 30 looks like the same amount of zoom as going from 30 to 15, and a linear ramp between two angles an octave apart therefore appears to race at the wide end and crawl at the narrow one. This shot spans roughly a factor of five, which is far enough for that to be the difference between a move and a lurch.

At 0.06 rad/s a shot held for swept sixty-nine degrees before cutting away, which looks like the camera sliding sideways past a building rather than going round it; 0.12 carries it through about a hundred and forty, far enough that two different faces of the subject come into view and the motion is legible as a circle.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Presentation.Cameras.MenuCameraLibrary
member.summary: Loads the per-mission menu-camera orbits from Assets/menu-cameras.json.
member.remarks: The file maps a mission id to a ; a mission with no entry, or a missing file, falls back to . Keeping the numbers in data means the showcase camera for a level can be re-tuned by flying the free camera with -camlog and editing the JSON, with no rebuild — the same "data, not code" reasoning the fog presets and LUTs follow.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Presentation.Cameras.MenuShowcaseCamera
member.summary: The slow orbital camera behind the menu, circling one location at a time and moving on to the next after a while.

remarks.para: A circular path around a point is the simplest spline that reads as "cinematic and alive" behind a menu, and it advances on real elapsed time, never a simulation tick, so it drifts smoothly however fast the frame runs. The orbit faces its centre throughout, tilted down by the authored pitch, which is what keeps the level filling the frame while the camera moves.

It circles a place rather than the level. Given several places () it holds each for and then moves to the next, so a mission is shown as a handful of establishing shots instead of one distant survey of the whole map. The move is a cut, not a fly-through: a path between two points a level apart would run through terrain and buildings, where a cut costs nothing and — dissolved into by the caller — reads as deliberate.
The cut is not taken by the camera itself. says a move is wanted and performs it, so the caller can hold the outgoing frame first and dissolve the two together. Nothing happens until it does.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Presentation.Cameras.MissionEntryCamera
member.summary: The single continuous shot that carries the player from the menu into their own eyes: the interface fades, the camera rises out of the menu's orbit to a top-down vantage, travels across the level to the mission's start, holds, and then drops in behind the character's head and becomes their view.

remarks.para: It owns no device, no renderer and no loop. Poses and a clock go in; a and a handful of presentation numbers come out. That is what lets the whole of it be tested without a graphics context, which matters because almost everything that can be wrong with a camera move is wrong in the arithmetic rather than in the drawing.

Where the weight comes from. Every phase eases, and which curve each one uses is a decision rather than a default. The rise carries the largest rotation in the shot — some eighty degrees, from the orbit's gentle downward tilt to nearly straight down — and a cubic in-out spends enough of itself near both ends that the camera appears to be heavy. The travel is a long flat move where a cubic would spend the whole phase accelerating and decelerating and never appear to cruise, so it takes a quadratic instead. The descent is cubic again, because arriving is the moment that most needs to slow.

The one thing that is not a tween. The menu's camera is moving when Play is pressed — it is a slow orbit, two to eight metres a second. Any tween that starts from a snapshot of that pose begins at zero velocity, so the picture visibly stops dead before the shot starts. The rise therefore blends against the live orbit for its first half-second, which preserves the orbit's velocity exactly at the moment of the cut and makes the move look like a continuation rather than a new shot. That is why is given the live showcase pose every frame.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Presentation.Cameras.MissionEntryCamera.ApexPitch
member.summary: The pitch held at altitude, in radians — eighty-five degrees down, not ninety.
member.remarks: At exactly straight down the yaw stops meaning anything and the frame reads flat and airless. Five degrees off keeps a sliver of horizon, keeps the buildings showing their sides, and keeps the heading legible as the camera travels — which is what makes it read as a map rather than a plan.

member.remarks: Below this a spawn just over the ridge would barely leave the ground.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Presentation.Cameras.MissionEntryCamera.MaximumApexRise
member.summary: The highest the shot will climb above the ground, in metres.
member.remarks: Well inside the far plane, and inside the range the shadow cascades are fitted over.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Presentation.Cameras.MissionEntryCamera.OrbitBlendSeconds
member.summary: How long the rise spends blending out of the live orbit, in seconds.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Presentation.Cameras.MissionEntryCamera.ApproachBehind
member.summary: How far behind and above the head the descent aims before it lands, in metres.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Presentation.Cameras.MissionEntryCamera.BodyHiddenWithin
member.summary: How close the camera gets to the eye before the standing body is taken away, in metres.

remarks.para: Far enough out that the character is still a figure standing in the level when it goes, rather than an object arriving at the lens. The descent ends AT the eye, which is inside the head, and the last stretch of it is fast — so a threshold measured in arm's lengths means the body sweeps from waist-height to filling the screen and then vanishes, all within a few frames. That reads as the character flashing, which is precisely what it is.

Taking it away at six metres costs nothing: the camera crosses the remaining distance in a small fraction of a second, by which point it is looking at where the character's head was rather than at the character, and there is nothing left to notice going.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Presentation.Cameras.MissionEntryCamera.HoldPatienceSeconds
member.summary: How long a hold may extend before the shot gives up waiting and lands anyway, in seconds.
member.remarks: The same patience the warm-up gate has: a first-time play of a mission bakes its distance field behind the hold, and the slowest measured bake is about seven seconds. Past this an honest hitch is better than a camera that hangs.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Presentation.Cameras.MissionEntryCamera.MotionBlur
member.summary: Gets how much the frame's own movement smears, 0 none to 1 fully.

remarks.para: A real camera's shutter is open for part of a frame, so anything that moves across it during that time is smeared — and this camera moves further in a second than a player ever will. Without it the travel across the level reads as a slideshow of sharp stills, which is the single biggest thing separating a camera move that looks shot from one that looks stepped.

Shaped per phase rather than derived from the camera's speed, because the speed varies by two orders of magnitude across the shot — hundreds of metres a second at altitude against walking pace at the landing — and any normalisation of that ends up being a hand-authored curve wearing a disguise. Strongest across the travel, backed off over the hold so the beat is legible, and exactly zero by the hand-over: gameplay gets the player's own setting back, and a smear still running on the first frame they control would be the shot overstaying.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Presentation.Cameras.MissionEntryCamera.PeakMotionBlur
member.summary: The widest the shot's own smear gets.
member.remarks:
Above the ultra preset's own 0.4, because this is a camera move rather than a player turning their head and the whole point of it is to read as shot rather than stepped.
An earlier value here was chosen by looking at a washed-out vantage and blaming the smear for it. That was impossible — motion blur was doing nothing at all at the time, for the reason recorded in GLGraphicsDevice.BeginSceneCapture — so the haze was the depth of field and the fog, and the conclusion drawn from it was worthless. Tuned again against an effect that actually runs.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Presentation.Cameras.MissionShowcasePoints
member.summary: Picks the handful of buildings in a mission worth looking at: three spread into a triangle across the level, and one or two more standing inside it, each framed close enough to read as a shot of that building.

remarks.para: A place is a building. Not a crate, not a tree, not a parked helicopter — the level itself says which is which. Level scripts name their placing tasks, and a structure is placed by a task called Building_1112 where a prop is an EditRigidObj or a Heli_353. That is a statement of intent by whoever built the level and no heuristic over triangle counts is going to beat it, so it is read directly and everything else is thrown away. The size and detail tests survive underneath it, because a level names a doorway a building too. A level that uses no such names — a mod's, most likely — falls back to judging the geometry alone, which is what the tests were doing on their own before.

Three shots in a triangle, not five in a compound. Ranking buildings and walking down the list with an exclusion radius, which is what this used to do, gives whatever the ranking likes best and then its nearest permitted neighbours: on mission 1 that was four shots inside a hundred and fifty metres of each other, four views of one yard. Spread is not something a greedy walk arrives at, so it is solved for instead: every triple of candidates is scored on how far apart its three corners are and how close to equilateral they sit, and the best one wins. What comes out is three establishing shots taken from three different parts of the map, which is what a menu backdrop is for.

Then the middle, if there is a middle. A triangle drawn across a sprawling airbase has a great deal of level inside it and the shots should visit some of it; one drawn across a level barely bigger than the triangle itself has nothing in the middle but the three corners seen again. So the interior shots are conditional on the room being there — measured as the triangle's inradius — and on a building standing well clear of all three edges. A mission that does not earn them gets three shots, which is the honest answer.

Close, not wide. The orbit comes from the building's own mesh and sits a little over it, so the subject fills the frame while the camera turns. Sizing shots from a cluster's statistics, as the first attempt did, produced orbits wider than the distance between them — every shot took in the whole area and the camera never actually looked at anything.

A level with no buildings at all falls back to the player's spawn, which is the one location in a mission that is not a spoiler by definition — it is where the player is about to be standing. Mission 14 is the only one that needs it: its scene holds a single object.

Everything here is deterministic — a ranking, an exhaustive search over a bounded shortlist, no seeding and no iteration — so a level always shows the same places in the same order. A menu that framed a different corner each time it opened would read as a bug.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Presentation.Cameras.MissionShowcasePoints.BuildingTaskPrefix

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Presentation.Cameras.MissionShowcasePoints.FewestDeclaredBuildings
member.summary: How many declared buildings a level needs before its own naming is trusted over the geometry.
member.remarks: Enough to draw the triangle out of. Below that the level either does not follow the convention or has almost nothing in it, and in both cases judging the meshes is the better answer than obeying two names.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Presentation.Cameras.MissionShowcasePoints.MinimumStructureRadius

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Presentation.Cameras.MissionShowcasePoints.MaximumStructureRadius
member.summary: The largest a model may be, in metres; past this it is a compound, not a building.
member.remarks: A 45-metre radius is a 90-metre building, which is already a hangar. Letting it go higher puts the orbit at its clamp and gives back the wide view that circling a place was meant to replace.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Presentation.Cameras.MissionShowcasePoints.MinimumTriangles
member.summary: The fewest triangles a structure may have, so a big flat plane is not mistaken for one.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Presentation.Cameras.MissionShowcasePoints.NeighbourhoodMetres
member.summary: How far around a structure counts as its neighbourhood, in metres.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Presentation.Cameras.MissionShowcasePoints.MinimumNeighbours
member.summary: How much has to stand within a structure's neighbourhood before it counts as somewhere.
member.remarks: A building alone in a field is a building but it is not a location. Low, because the corners of the triangle are by definition at the edges of the built-up area and a strict count would pull all three back into the middle of the base — which is the shot this was written to stop producing.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Presentation.Cameras.MissionShowcasePoints.ShortlistCellsAcross
member.summary: How many cells across the level's candidates are bucketed for the triangle search.
member.remarks: The search is exhaustive over triples, so its input has to be bounded: one candidate per cell of an 8×8 grid caps it at 64 corners and around forty thousand triples, which is nothing. Bucketing by PLACE rather than taking the top 64 by rank is the point — the highest-ranked buildings in a level are all in the same compound, so a rank-based shortlist would hand the search the very clustering it exists to undo.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Presentation.Cameras.MissionShowcasePoints.FamilyRepeatPenalty
member.summary: How much a triple is discounted for showing the same kind of building twice.
member.remarks: A level places one prefab a dozen times, and a search that only wanted distance happily picked three copies of the same hut standing far apart: three corners, one building, which is what made the whole thing look broken. A discount rather than a ban, so a level built out of one prefab still gets its three shots.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Presentation.Cameras.MissionShowcasePoints.CompactTriangleSide
member.summary: The side length, in metres, below which the best triangle is really one compound.
member.remarks: Reported, not enforced: a small level still gets the best triple it has.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Presentation.Cameras.MissionShowcasePoints.InteriorInradiusMetres
member.summary: How much room the triangle needs inside it, as an inradius in metres, to be worth filling.
member.remarks: The largest circle that fits between the three corners, which is the honest measure of whether the middle is somewhere else or just the corners seen again — a long thin triangle has plenty of area and no middle at all. A little under twice the tightest orbit, so a shot placed in there is looking at its own subject rather than at the ones on either side of it.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Presentation.Cameras.MissionShowcasePoints.InteriorMargin
member.summary: How far off every edge an interior building must stand, in barycentric terms.
member.remarks: A barycentric coordinate is the fraction of the way across the triangle from the opposite edge, so requiring all three above this keeps an interior shot clear of the edges and out of the corners — a building just inside one edge is a fourth view of the corner shot next to it.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Presentation.Cameras.MissionShowcasePoints.InteriorGapFraction
member.summary: How far an interior shot must stand from the corners, as a fraction of the shortest side.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Presentation.Cameras.MissionShowcasePoints.InteriorMinimumGap
member.summary: The closest an interior shot may ever come to another shot, in metres.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Presentation.Cameras.MissionShowcasePoints.MaximumInteriorPoints
member.summary: The most shots taken from inside the triangle.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Presentation.Cameras.MissionShowcasePoints.Extract(OpenIGI.Game.World.WorldScene,OpenIGI.Engine.Tasks.GameTask,System.Int32,OpenIGI.Presentation.Cameras.MenuCameraSpec,OpenIGI.Core.Diagnostics.IOpenIgiLogger)
member.summary: Finds the places in a mission worth showing.
member.param: The built scene, for its placements.
The level's task tree, for the player's spawn; may be .
The most places to return; three of them are the triangle's corners.
The orbit style each place's own orbit is based on.
Where to report what was found.
member.returns: Up to places: the triangle first, then its interior.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Presentation.Cameras.MissionShowcasePoints.SpawnOnly(OpenIGI.Engine.Tasks.GameTask,OpenIGI.Presentation.Cameras.MenuCameraSpec)
member.summary: The player's spawn, orbited close, for a level with nothing standing in it to circle.
member.remarks: A last resort, not a shot anyone chose. Mission 14 puts a single object in its scene, so there is no building to find and no triangle to draw; without this the backdrop falls back to a wide orbit around the median of every placement, which on a level with one placement is a survey of empty ground. The spawn at least frames where the player is about to be standing.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Presentation.Cameras.MissionShowcasePoints.HeightBandSpreads
member.summary: How many interquartile ranges either side of the median a structure may sit.
member.remarks: The usual outlier rule. Three is loose rather than tight, because the point is to reject things a kilometre away, not to trim a hilltop.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Presentation.Cameras.MissionShowcasePoints.NarrowestHeightBandMetres
member.summary: The narrowest the band may be, for a level whose placements sit on one plane.
member.remarks: A flat level has an interquartile range near nought, and three times nought would refuse every building that stands up. Eighty metres is taller than anything either game places on the ground.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Presentation.Cameras.MissionShowcasePoints.HeightBand(OpenIGI.Game.World.WorldScene)
member.summary: The band of heights the level's own placements occupy, ignoring its outliers.

remarks.para: Percentiles rather than min and max, because the outliers are exactly what this is for. The band is relative to the level, so a mission that is genuinely ten kilometres up is described correctly -- location1/level3's placements sit around 9,939 m and its band goes with them.

Why it is needed. I.G.I. 2's first mission is a parachute drop, and it places the aircraft: a 14,793-triangle c-130bay at 4,630 m, with drop props at 15,140 m, over a level whose own placements run from about -17 to +39 m. Picked by triangle count and model radius alone -- which is all this did -- the backdrop orbited the aeroplane, four and a half kilometres up, against an empty sky. Project I.G.I. never showed it because nothing in it is placed a kilometre above the ground.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Presentation.Cameras.MissionShowcasePoints.FindBuildings(OpenIGI.Game.World.WorldScene,OpenIGI.Core.Diagnostics.IOpenIgiLogger)
member.summary: Every placement in a level that is a building, measured and scored.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Presentation.Cameras.MissionShowcasePoints.PickTriangle(System.Collections.Generic.List{OpenIGI.Presentation.Cameras.MissionShowcasePoints.Structure},OpenIGI.Core.Diagnostics.IOpenIgiLogger)
member.summary: Solves for the three buildings that spread widest and sit most evenly around the level.
member.remarks: Exhaustive over the shortlist rather than greedy. A greedy walk takes the best-ranked building and then whatever else it is allowed, which on every retail level is the rest of the same compound; only looking at the triple as a whole can trade a slightly duller building for one that is four hundred metres away.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Presentation.Cameras.MissionShowcasePoints.Shortlist(System.Collections.Generic.List{OpenIGI.Presentation.Cameras.MissionShowcasePoints.Structure})

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Presentation.Cameras.MissionShowcasePoints.TightenOverlappingShots(System.Collections.Generic.List{OpenIGI.Presentation.Cameras.ShowcasePoint})
member.summary: Pulls each orbit in until it cannot take in the subject of another shot.
member.param: The chosen places; their orbits are narrowed in place.
member.remarks: A backstop rather than the normal path, now that the shots are solved for spread: two of them can still end up close on a level with nowhere else to put them, and two orbits that overlap are one shot shown twice. Rather than drop a place for being too near its neighbour, its orbit is pulled in to just under half the distance between them.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Presentation.Cameras.MissionShowcasePoints.ModelRadiusMetres(OpenIGI.Formats.World.MefModel)
member.summary: The radius of a model's own mesh, in metres.
member.remarks: The horizontal extent, not the full three-dimensional one: the orbit is a circle on the ground, so what decides how far out it has to sit is how wide the building is, not how tall. A radio mast framed by its height would be circled from three hundred metres away.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Presentation.Cameras.MissionShowcasePoints.Structure.Family
member.summary: Gets the model's family — everything before the first underscore of its name.
member.remarks: A pack names a model 418_01_1 and 418_02_1, which are two pieces or two variants of one structure. Keeping the shots distinct by full model name lets both through and puts what is visibly the same building on screen twice; the family is what actually has to differ.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Presentation.Cameras.MissionShowcasePoints.Structure.Score
member.summary: How good a subject this is: how detailed, how big, and how busy around it.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Presentation.Cameras.MissionShowcasePoints.Structure.ToPoint(OpenIGI.Presentation.Cameras.MenuCameraSpec)
member.summary: Turns the building into a shot of itself: an orbit sized to the mesh, close in.

remarks.para: The distance is a multiple of the building's own radius plus a fixed margin, never a flat number: a fixed one either stands a shed off at a hundred metres or drives the camera through a hangar's wall. At 1.3× plus nine metres a small building is watched from a dozen metres off its wall and a large one from around twenty — close enough to read as a shot of that building rather than of the area it stands in, and still outside anything the level puts against it.

The height is deliberately low against the radius. A tall orbit looks down at a roof, and what makes a building read is its elevation; a third of the radius keeps the camera tilted about twenty degrees down, which sees the front of a wall and the ground it stands on at once.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Presentation.Cameras.ShowcasePointFile
member.summary: Writes Assets/menu-cameras.json from places found in the levels, so the shots a mission's backdrop cycles between become reviewable, editable data rather than something recomputed every run.

remarks.para: The file is generated by -poidump and then owned by hand. Everything in it can be edited — a place moved a few metres, an orbit pulled in, a dull one replaced — and nothing regenerates it behind the author's back; a mission with no entry falls back to finding its places at load, which is what keeps a mod's levels working without anybody running the tool.

Written by hand rather than through so the result is laid out for a person to read and diff: one place per line, coordinates to one decimal, missions in campaign order. A serialiser's output is correct and unreadable, and this file's whole purpose is to be edited.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Presentation.DeferredLighting
member.summary: What a title whose levels author their own light hands the dynamic renderer, in place of what it would otherwise derive from where the sun is in the sky.
member.param: The flat fill the level authors, which is the sequel's GlobalLight object ambient rather than the Dirlight's back colour. Nineteen of the sequel's twenty-four levels leave that back colour at black, so the ambient the dynamic path used was nothing at all.
How dark the level is meant to read, nought for full day and one for full night. Drives the exposure, and nothing else.

remarks.para: Why a title needs this at all. Project I.G.I. authors a sun as a position in the sky, and the dynamic path treats it as one: it decomposes the authored direction into an elevation and a bearing, sweeps it around an arc for the time of day, fades its colour out as it sets, and reads the picture's darkness off how far below the horizon it has gone. All of that is sound for a game whose levels are outdoors at a stated hour.

I.G.I. 2 does not author a sun. It authors a lighting DIRECTION and puts the darkness in the colour. Measured over all twenty-four of its levels: the first mission's sun stands well up the sky and is very nearly black (0.10, 0.15, 0.25) because the mission is at night. Fed to a model that reads darkness off elevation, that comes out exactly backwards — the night mission is lit as noon.

So a title that answers this is saying: my sun is where I put it, my ambient is what I wrote, and how dark the scene is does not follow from either. A title that answers nothing keeps the sky model exactly as it was, which is what Project I.G.I. does and what its regression captures depend on.

What this deliberately does NOT carry is a direction. It used to say so on the grounds that five of the sequel's levels authored a sun below the horizon, four of them bright — and that was the READER's fault, not the data's. DirectionFrom took the forward row of an Euler composition, which discards Gamma and swaps elevation for zenith; read as both binaries read it, not one of the twenty-four points underground. The underground suns are gone and so is that argument.

It still carries no direction, for the reason that survived: retail BAKES. Its directional light reaches only the objects with no lightmap, so where it points barely shows, and the sweep's own arc is what the rest of the frame is calibrated against. Changing that is a picture decision with its own evidence to gather, not a correction to make in passing — so this carries the two things the level measurably says and leaves the arc alone.

member.param: Where the level sits on the day/night cycle, for one it authors as a NIGHT. Null for a level whose authored lighting is already a daytime one: seven of the thirteen Project I.G.I. missions with a sky (the other six paint a night dome) and nineteen of the sequel's twenty-four.

param.name: CompleteBake
param.para: Whether the level's shipped bakes are a WHOLE lighting solution, direct light included.

The hybrid model adds a live sun on top of the bakes, because its premise is that a bake is an AMBIENT term -- the bounce and the fill, with the key light left to be computed. That is a statement about the bakes, and it is not true of every game's.

I.G.I. 2's are whole: the ground's third pass is a full lighting solution and a lightmapped object carries one too, which is why the fixed-function sun reaches only the objects that have NO bake. Adding a sun over them counts the key light twice, and on its night missions it does so at a scale that swamps the bake -- the directional there is the level's own night sun, some thirty times the moon the cycle invents for a level without one. Measured on mission 1, hybrid came out at 3.5 times vanilla's ground with the night exposure on and 6.9 with it off, against a baked model at 0.18.
A title that says its bakes are whole has the hybrid model's added sun withheld, so hybrid reproduces the bake rather than doubling it. Project I.G.I. says nothing and keeps the sun it always had.

member.param: How much exposure the level's night takes off at full night, or null for the renderer's own figure, which was fitted against I.G.I. 2's nearly black night suns. A title whose nights are lit by the cycle's moon has its darkness computed already, and says how much less to take off on top.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Presentation.AuthoredNight
member.summary: Where a level whose authored lighting IS a night sits on the day/night cycle.
member.param: The hour at which the cycle reproduces the level's authored lighting.
The sun to sweep UP to, which a night level does not author.
The fill to sweep up to, likewise.

remarks.para: The cycle assumes a level authors its sun at noon and sweeps down from there: it fits an arc through the authored elevation at the authored hour, fades the sun out as that arc sets, hangs a moon on the anti-solar point and crosses the fill to a night blue. Handed a level that authors a NIGHT, all of that is applied to a scene that is already dark -- the sun is faded from nearly black to black, and an authored night fill is crossed towards another one.

I.G.I. 2's night levels are exactly that, and they are worse than that: they leave the sun a third of the way UP the sky and paint it (0.10, 0.15, 0.25), so nothing about their elevation says night and the arc cannot be made to say it either -- an arc through an above-horizon elevation at a night hour has no solution, and the fit's own clamp rejects it.

So a level answering this is bound to the cycle by its NIGHT end instead of its day one. Its authored sun becomes the cycle's moon and its authored fill the cycle's night fill, reached at -- where the picture is then exactly what its artists made. The day end is what it never authored and has to be supplied: sweeping to noon lights it with and .

Whether the authored sun IS the moon depends on the title. I.G.I. 2 paints its night sun nearly black, which is a night's light and is used as the moon as it stands. Project I.G.I. says night only with its sky dome and leaves the Dirlight the same near-white noon sun every level authors, which as a moon lights the night as brightly as a dim day -- so there is false and the cycle keeps its own faint moon, taking only the direction.

member.param: Whether the authored sun's colour is the night's moonlight.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Presentation.AuthoredNight.#ctor(System.Single,OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3f,OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3f,System.Boolean)
member.summary: Where a level whose authored lighting IS a night sits on the day/night cycle.
member.param: The hour at which the cycle reproduces the level's authored lighting.
The sun to sweep UP to, which a night level does not author.
The fill to sweep up to, likewise.

remarks.para: The cycle assumes a level authors its sun at noon and sweeps down from there: it fits an arc through the authored elevation at the authored hour, fades the sun out as that arc sets, hangs a moon on the anti-solar point and crosses the fill to a night blue. Handed a level that authors a NIGHT, all of that is applied to a scene that is already dark -- the sun is faded from nearly black to black, and an authored night fill is crossed towards another one.

I.G.I. 2's night levels are exactly that, and they are worse than that: they leave the sun a third of the way UP the sky and paint it (0.10, 0.15, 0.25), so nothing about their elevation says night and the arc cannot be made to say it either -- an arc through an above-horizon elevation at a night hour has no solution, and the fit's own clamp rejects it.

So a level answering this is bound to the cycle by its NIGHT end instead of its day one. Its authored sun becomes the cycle's moon and its authored fill the cycle's night fill, reached at -- where the picture is then exactly what its artists made. The day end is what it never authored and has to be supplied: sweeping to noon lights it with and .

Whether the authored sun IS the moon depends on the title. I.G.I. 2 paints its night sun nearly black, which is a night's light and is used as the moon as it stands. Project I.G.I. says night only with its sky dome and leaves the Dirlight the same near-white noon sun every level authors, which as a moon lights the night as brightly as a dim day -- so there is false and the cycle keeps its own faint moon, taking only the direction.

member.summary: Binds the level's sun to the cycle.
member.param: The sun exactly as the level wrote it.
What the title says about the level, or null for a title that says nothing.
member.returns: The sun to hand the cycle.

remarks.para: The cycle's contract is that a level authors its sun at NOON and it sweeps down from there. Project I.G.I. honours that and comes back unchanged. I.G.I. 2 does not, in two ways, and both have to be answered here or the cycle is meaningless on it.

First, its FILL. The sequel leaves the Dirlight's back colour black in nineteen of its twenty-four levels and puts the real ambient on GlobalLight instead, so the cycle would cross to black at noon. The title's answer replaces it, and the cycle then has a real daytime fill to reach.

Second, its NIGHT levels. They paint the sun nearly black and leave it a third of the way UP the sky, so the arc cannot be fitted to say night -- and must not be asked to, because what they author IS the night. Such a level is turned round: the cycle is handed the ANTI-solar direction at midnight, where its own moon flips it back and returns the authored direction exactly, with the authored colour and fill supplied separately as the night to cross to. What it sweeps UP to is the daytime the level never wrote, which the title supplies from the levels that did.

Why the turn-round works. The arc fits its peak elevation as referenceElevation / sin(referencePhase) and clamps it positive. Handed the authored elevation at a night hour that quotient is negative and the clamp rejects it, which is the dead end. Handed the NEGATED elevation at the same hour both signs cancel, the fit lands on the authored elevation, and at that hour the arc reproduces it pointing the other way -- which is exactly what the moon path then flips back.

member.summary: Takes a point of the world to the pixel it is drawn at, as the frame's own projection takes it.
member.remarks: The world-to-view step is the camera's own (): the subtraction in double precision, then the orientation's rows. member.name: T:OpenIGI.Presentation.Hud.Remastered.HudReactiveState
member.summary: What the display does about what changed since the last frame: it shakes and flashes when the player is hit, lets the health it lost fall away behind it, rolls its round counter to the new count, slides a new weapon in, pulses when the player can be seen, and flickers a part in as it appears.
member.remarks: Driven by the seconds it is handed, not the wall clock, so a frame captured at a given simulation time draws the same every run.

member.summary: How much of a part shows at a density: all of it at full; at contextual and minimal, all of it for a while after something about it changed, then dimming to a ghost -- or to nothing at minimal -- unless what it shows is urgent. The inventory never dims: what the player carries is always to be read at a glance.

The density.
The frame's model, for what is urgent.
member.returns: Its opacity, nought to one.

member.summary: The titles' pictures as the remastered display draws them: each a copy of the title's own, sampled smoothly, so a weapon drawn larger than its art -- on the weapon wheel, say -- is smooth rather than blocky.
member.remarks: The titles upload their art for nearest-texel sampling (), right for the original displays, which draw it pixel for pixel; those keep theirs. A copy is made the first time a picture is drawn here, and kept until the display is let go.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Presentation.Hud.Remastered.RemasteredHud
member.summary: The remastered heads-up display, shared by both titles: each fills a from its own player and hands it in with its own , and this draws it in that title's look, at its places, through the visor.

remarks.para: The display is drawn into a layer of its own () and laid over the frame by one pass that bends, fringes, lines, lights and shakes it (); on a device without the layer, or with the effects off, it is drawn straight over the frame, flat. The glass the groups stand on samples the frame as it was before the display, blurred.
One instance keeps the reactive state for one player's display: what changed since the last frame is what it animates.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Presentation.Hud.Remastered.Widgets.HudAlertBanner
member.summary: One small line at the top of the screen saying how far the soldiers are onto the player, in the title's own terms: SEARCHING, SUSPICIOUS, ALARM, DETECTED. Nothing is drawn over the soldiers themselves.
member.remarks: The word sits between two short rules over a faint dark band, in the colour its status calls for: amber while they search, pale while they wonder, the theme's danger for an alarm or a sighting. A new status comes up with a flash -- DETECTED with a slice of it slipping now and then, ALARM with its mark blinking -- and one cleared lingers a moment, fading ().

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Presentation.Hud.Remastered.Widgets.HudCrosshair
member.summary: The remastered crosshair: a few short white ticks that sit where the weapon's rounds may land and close in as its aim steadies -- three for most guns, left, right and below, with no centre point while aiming; a circle for a shotgun; three with four small diagonals near the centre for a scoped rifle fired from the hip; a faint point for a knife. A hit shows a small cross that blinks off; a kill a larger red one that holds, punching out again if another kill lands while it shows. Not retail.
member.remarks: The ticks are offset from the centre by the projected spread itself (the cone's half-angle as the view sees it), so a tight weapon brings them almost together and a wild one throws them wide. The drawing is this port's own.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Presentation.Hud.Remastered.Widgets.HudWheel
member.summary: The weapon wheel, in the theme's colours: a ring of glass sectors round the aim, one a weapon, lit at the rim; the one pointed at lifts out, brightens and throws a glow past the ring; a dial of ticks runs round the outside, brightest where the mouse points, with a few arcs turning slowly beyond it; the middle shows the weapon pointed at, large, with its name and rounds.

remarks.para: The world behind is the visor pass's to take out of time (drained, smeared and grained: Ui/HudFx.slang); where that pass is not running, the wheel lays its own blurred, darkened backdrop.

It opens turning in from a little behind, a little smaller, its sectors coming in one after another round the ring. The ring's first sector is straight up and the rest follow clockwise (). Sized by the screen's height rather than the theme's scale, so it is the same size in either game; its other measures are in wheel pixels, a 250th of its outer radius.

member.summary: Draws the lamp on each of a level's security cameras that shows what it is doing.
member.remarks: A sprite billboard per camera, coloured by the camera's state. The implementation is title content because the sprite it loads is named by an alias path belonging to one game, and a shared renderer may not know one — even though itself is shared. The architecture test enforces exactly that, and caught this remark quoting the path when it was first written.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Presentation.IHudPresenter
member.summary: Draws a title's heads-up display, in the shape the original drew it.

remarks.para: Rule 3 of docs/architecture.md names a HUD element as title content outright, and this is why: the ammunition counter, the health bar, the sniper scope and the action badge are one game's own layout, drawn from one game's own font and sprite archives. Nothing about the shape of a status screen carries to another game.

The two HUD presenters are alternatives, not layers: this one reproduces the original's, and is the modern reskin the r_hud_remastered setting selects between. holds the predicates that choose, and is title-agnostic because choosing between two styles is not itself a style.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Presentation.IMapComputerPresenter
member.summary: Draws a title's handheld map computer.

remarks.para: Title content twice over: the device is one game's own model and screens, and its pages are laid out from that game's own string archives. ITitleDataLayout.StringArchives is where those paths live now, so the shell can preload them without naming a renderer.
is the modern alternative to this, chosen by a setting, the same way the two HUDs are alternatives. They share so the host can frame the world behind either without knowing which it has.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Presentation.IMapComputerPresenter.MapAvailable
member.summary: Gets or sets whether the level lets the player have the map page at all.
member.remarks: The level's HumanPlayerInput carries a "Mapcomputer on expression", evaluated every tick (0x45DCF0). Without the device the computer still opens, on its objectives page (0x46BB10 passes mode 2 to 0x46AFB0), and neither text page offers a MAP link (0x468920, 0x468E90). Missions 7 and 14 never have it, mission 8 gains it with GenericPickup 860, and mission 13 loses it inside AreaActivate 3999.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Presentation.ScenePresentationRequest
member.summary: What a title needs in order to build the things standing in its world.
member.param: The graphics device to upload through.
The level's task tree, which is what declares them.
The registry the level's own files are read from.

Resolves a model by the name a level refers to it by, or returns when there is none. A host that has not opened the mission's model packs supplies a lookup that always declines, and the passes that need geometry then build nothing rather than half of something.

Resolves a model name and one of its material slots to the texture that slot samples, or when nothing answers. A mesh alone cannot say: a material belongs to the instance that uses the mesh, and only the packs know which instance that is.
Where load diagnostics go.
The session's services, which hold the title's graphics options when it keeps them.

remarks.para: The model lookup is the whole reason this is a separate request. A ground reads its own height fields out of an archive and a sky builds its dome from nothing, so needs the registry and no more. A forest does not: it plants instances of a model, thousands of them, and the model lives in a pack the mission opened rather than in the level's own files. Widening the ground's request to carry a lookup it never uses would have made every title implementing a ground answer for one it does not need.

A delegate rather than the pack list itself, because the two games disagree about packs — how many, in what order, and which wins a name that appears in more than one — and none of that disagreement belongs above the seam. What both agree on is that a name resolves to a mesh, or does not.

member.remarks: Both a file system and a registry, because the two games fetch a cloud texture differently: one layer names a path its virtual file system resolves directly, and the other names a bare file the engine rebases into the mission's own texture directory and reads through the registry. Handing over both and letting each title take the one it uses is smaller than an abstraction over "somewhere a texture comes from", and it keeps the alias vocabulary on the titles' side of the seam where the layering rules put it.

member.summary: What one frame needs in order to draw a title's sky.
member.param: The camera the sky is drawn about.
The view-to-clip transform.
The level's elapsed time, which scrolls the clouds.
member.remarks: Seconds rather than ticks, and that is a compromise worth naming. Both games advance a cloud layer's scroll per simulation tick — I.G.I. 2's FlatSkyLayer_RunHandler is read and does exactly that — so a tick count is what a presenter really wants. The host's own clock is a wall clock, and giving the seam a tick count it would have to invent would move the guess rather than remove it. A presenter that knows its title's tick rate converts; one that does not says so.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Presentation.ISkyPresenter
member.summary: Draws a title's sky: whatever backdrop stands behind the world.

remarks.para: An interface because the host was building one game's sky by name. SkyRenderer finds its FlatSky by walking the tree for a DeclaredTask called that, which is how a title with no class for the type carries it — and I.G.I. 2 has a class for it, so the same walk finds nothing and the sequel drew no sky at all. The two also disagree about where a layer's texture comes from and about how large the dome is. None of that is the host's business.

The properties are the ones a frame needs from a sky that are not drawing: the fog colour is what the frame clears to, so the horizon meets sky-coloured backing rather than black, and the fog amount and plane height seed the volumetric fog. They are on the interface rather than behind a describe method because the host acts on them, unlike 's counters, which it only prints.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Presentation.ISkyPresenter.IsGameOwnSky
member.summary: Gets whether this sky is the game's own painted one, to be kept rather than replaced.

remarks.para: True for a sky whose colours are the ones the artist wanted on the screen and whose mood is authored per mission. A deferred frame otherwise substitutes its own atmosphere wherever no geometry wrote depth, which a sky dome never does — and an atmosphere cannot be a night sky for a game that authors night in the sun's COLOUR rather than its height.

Defaulted to FALSE rather than true, though both games' skies are painted. Project I.G.I.'s deferred picture is a regression gate and its atmosphere is deliberate — the remaster replaces that game's flat gradient on purpose. Turning this on for it is its own decision, not a side effect of the sequel asking.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Presentation.ITerrainPresenter
member.summary: Draws a title's ground.

remarks.para: Terrain is the first pass to get an interface of its own because it is where the two games diverge hardest. I.G.I. 1's ground is a chunked octree streamed by level of detail out of .ctr and .cmd; I.G.I. 2's is a flat grid of tiles, each a .thm height field with a material and a lightmap beside it. Almost nothing about one describes the other, which is exactly the condition that makes an interface worth extracting rather than a shared base class.

The counters are behind rather than on properties for the same reason. A chunk count, an octree visit count and a batch-page occupancy are facts about I.G.I. 1's implementation, and a developer overlay that named them would be an overlay only I.G.I. 1 could fill. Lines of text are what the overlay actually wants and all it should be promised.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Presentation.GroundPresentationRequest
member.summary: Builds the renderers one title draws with.

remarks.para: A separate seam from because the reference graph forbids joining them: OpenIGI.Presentation references OpenIGI.Engine, so Engine cannot name a presenter. The composition root resolves both from the same title and is the only place that names either implementation, which is the property that actually matters.

It grows one method per pass as each pass stops being constructed by the host: terrain, then the world, then the first-person and projectile passes. The HUD, the map computer and the cameras are what is left, plus the two that are not getting interfaces at all — see the census on TitleContentTests for which and why.

member.remarks: Nothing here is title-shaped, which is the point: a title is handed the level and reads whatever its own ground happens to be, rather than being handed a ground somebody else decided the shape of.

remarks.para: Every factory may return null, and the default is null. That is the same rule already states for the passes themselves: a title under construction presents what it has and skips the rest. The interface was written when one title existed, so returning non-null everywhere cost nothing; a second title makes the difference real — I.G.I. 2 can draw its world today and has no view model, no HUD and no map computer, because those are milestones that have not happened yet.

A default of null rather than an abstract member is deliberate: it means a title implements the passes it has and stays silent about the others, instead of carrying thirteen overrides that all say "not yet". The host's own presenter fields are already nullable, so nothing downstream changes.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Presentation.ITitlePresentationProvider.ReadAtmosphere(OpenIGI.Engine.Tasks.GameTask)
member.summary: Reads the air this title's levels are played in, if it authors one.
member.param: The level's task tree.
member.returns: The atmosphere, or nothing when this game does not author one.

remarks.para: A title seam, and deliberately empty by default. I.G.I. 2 lights its levels with a GlobalLight task carrying a fog colour, a fog density and a flat ambient, and applies that fog to every surface it draws. Project I.G.I. has no such task and no such pass, and its picture is a regression gate — so it answers nothing here and the host applies nothing, which is what keeps a change to the sequel's air from reaching it at all rather than merely not being noticed.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Presentation.ITitlePresentationProvider.ReadObjectShading(OpenIGI.Engine.Tasks.GameTask)
member.summary: Reads how this title composites its placed objects, if it departs from the default.
member.param: The level's task tree.
member.returns: The shading, or nothing when this game draws objects the way the port always has.

remarks.para: A second seam rather than a wider first one. is about the air and is baked into every pipeline; this is about how a lightmap is applied and what lights an object without one, and is applied per draw. I.G.I. 2's lightmap stage is MODULATE2X and its unlightmapped objects are lit by Direct3D's own vertex pipeline from the level's sun ( cites the state blocks); Project I.G.I. answers nothing here and is composited exactly as before.

member.summary: Reads how this title's models give up detail with distance, if its renderer did so.
member.param: The level's task tree, which carries the level's settings.
Where the game's per-model distances are read from.
The session's services, which hold a title's own distances and detail options when it keeps them.
member.returns: The policy, or nothing to draw every model at its first level.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Presentation.ITitlePresentationProvider.ReadDeferredLighting(OpenIGI.Engine.Tasks.GameTask)
member.summary: Reads how this title's level drives the dynamic renderer, if it authors that itself.
member.param: The level's task tree.
member.returns: The lighting, or nothing when this game's sun is a position in the sky and the host should go on deriving the picture's darkness and its fill from where that position is.

remarks.para: A third seam, and the one that turns the sky model off. The other two are about what a surface is drawn with; this is about what lights it in the dynamic path. Answering it says three things at once: use my sun's direction as authored rather than sweeping it around an arc, fill with this ambient rather than the one you would have blended towards, and take this darkness rather than measuring my sun's height. gives the measurements behind that, over all of I.G.I. 2's levels.

Project I.G.I. answers nothing for a daylit level and keeps the sweep, the moon and the elevation-derived exposure untouched — which its regression captures require, since every one of them is a dynamic frame. It answers only for the six missions whose sky dome it paints as night, which its Dirlight cannot say: every level authors that sun at the same noon.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Presentation.WorldDrawOptions
member.summary: What one draw of the world should include.
member.param: Objects whose bounding radius is below this are skipped. The shadow cascades use it to drop casters too small to read at their resolution; a main pass passes zero.
Whether the previous frame's visibility results may reject objects.
Whether to draw only the level's glazing -- half of a texture on a placement whose other half went into the G-buffer, so it is a pass of its own rather than part of the rotor pass beside it.

Draws only the placements marks, and nothing else. A spinning rotor disc is alpha-blended and has to be laid over the world after the opaque pass rather than sorted into it, so the host issues a second draw for them. A title whose scenes mark no rotors draws nothing and costs a walk of the list.

Whether the pass is drawn from the frame's eye, so the title's view culling may narrow a placement to the part of the view it is seen through (). False for a light's view, which has no window onto anything.
Draws only the face groups the original sorts and blends (), over the opaque world, testing depth without writing it.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Presentation.IWorldPresenter
member.summary: Draws a title's static world geometry.

remarks.para: The host owns the frame and the order of its passes; the title owns what each pass draws. That is the original engine's own RenderMode seam moved up one level — the engine always drew through a registered mode, and it always drew this game's world through it.

This is a census, not a design. Every member is one the host already used on I.G.I. 1's world renderer, and there are exactly as many as it used — 24 of the 24 that class made public. Inventing a smaller surface would have meant leaving the host holding the concrete type for whatever was left out, which is the thing this interface exists to stop.

The bindings below are the part a second title will use least. They are what a level hands the world so it can animate the kinds of object that level contains, and every one is nullable for that exact reason: I.G.I. 2 declares no Elevator task at all, and a title binds what it has. A null binding is not a missing feature, it is a game without that kind of object in it.

member.remarks: A replacement pack is dropped in while the game runs and r_overrides is toggled; what it replaces has already been uploaded, so each presenter has to be told to read its own again. Defaulted to nothing, for a title that caches none.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Presentation.ITitlePresentation
member.summary: The renderers one title draws its world with.

remarks.para: Every presenter is nullable so that a title under construction renders the passes it has and skips the rest, rather than failing the frame. An I.G.I. 2 build with terrain but no characters is a useful build; one that will not present is not.

This carries the two passes that have a consumer today — draws the world and the characters into the sun's cascades, and it is the one place a pass is handed its renderers rather than reaching for them. The view model, the HUD and the menus are drawn by the host against concrete renderers still, and move behind this interface when there is a second implementation to shape them against: an abstraction extracted from one implementation is usually the wrong one, and the cost of widening this later is a method, not a redesign.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Presentation.WeaponDrawParts
member.summary: Which of a weapon's parts one call covers.
member.remarks: The split exists because the two kinds of part belong to different passes on the modern renderer: the gun's body is geometry, but its muzzle flame is LIGHT — additive, depth-read-only — and light drawn into the deferred G-buffer comes out shaded like scenery. That was visible as a one-frame dark square at a firing soldier's muzzle. A soldier now draws its body in the geometry and shadow passes and its flame in the forward pass; the first-person weapon draws whole in the forward pass and keeps .

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Presentation.Lighting.DistanceFieldValidation
member.summary: Checks a clipmap the GPU built against the exact answer the CPU can compute.

remarks.para: A distance field is a volume of plausible-looking numbers, and every way of building one wrongly produces a volume of equally plausible-looking numbers. Nothing downstream fails visibly either — a trace against a bad field does not error, it returns the wrong surface, and the first symptom is lighting that looks subtly off several stages later.

exists precisely so there is something to compare against: it answers the same question exactly, by consulting every object. This reads the clipmap back and asks both the same thing at the same world points.

What counts as agreement. The clipmap is a resampling, so it is allowed to differ by about what its own voxels can resolve. What it is not allowed to do is disagree about the sign, or report more free space than exists — the first means a trace cannot tell a wall from the air beside it, and the second means it steps straight through one.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Presentation.Lighting.DistanceFieldValidation.Read(OpenIGI.Rendering.IGraphicsDevice,OpenIGI.Presentation.Lighting.GlobalDistanceField,System.Int32,OpenIGI.Core.Diagnostics.IOpenIgiLogger)
member.summary: Reads one clipmap level back, through a compute shader.
member.remarks:
Not through glGetTexImage, and that is the whole point of this method existing. Measured on the driver this was developed against: glGetTexImage does not observe a compute shader's imageStore writes at all — not with TEXTURE_UPDATE, not with ALL_BARRIER_BITS, not after a finish, and with no GL error raised. A volume uploaded from memory reads back through that path perfectly, so what fails is specifically image-store visibility.
So the values come back the way the compute self-test already proves works: a shader reads the image and writes a storage buffer, which reads back correctly. Without this the validator reported every clipmap as entirely unwritten, and that false negative cost two stages.

member.summary: Compares one clipmap level against the exact field.

Which level to check, zero being the innermost.
Where to report the findings.
member.returns: What the comparison found.
member.remarks: Every voxel of the level is compared rather than a sample of them. It costs a readback and a few hundred thousand CPU evaluations, which is seconds — affordable because this runs when asked rather than every frame, and worth it because a fault confined to one corner of the volume is exactly the kind a sample would miss.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Presentation.Lighting.GlobalDistanceField
member.summary: The level's distance field resampled onto grids that follow the camera, so a trace step is one fetch.

remarks.para: gives the exact answer by consulting every object. A ray takes hundreds of steps and a frame traces millions of rays, so the exact answer is unaffordable per step. This resamples it onto a small volume around the camera: a step becomes one texture fetch, and how much geometry the level holds stops mattering.

Rebuilt rarely, and that is what makes it cheap. I.G.I.'s levels are static — nothing in them moves except doors and people, neither of which this describes — so a clipmap only becomes wrong when the camera walks out of it. Each level is snapped to its own voxel grid and rebuilt when the camera has moved a fraction of its extent, which for the outer levels is almost never.

Snapping is not an optimisation. A grid that follows the camera continuously resamples the same geometry onto slightly different voxel centres every frame, and the result flickers — the distance at a fixed world point changes because the grid moved under it. Snapping the origin to a multiple of the voxel size means a point keeps the same voxel until the grid jumps a whole voxel, and what was already computed stays valid.
All levels live in one volume texture stacked along z, so a trace binds one image and indexes it by level rather than binding four.

There is no separate per-mesh distance-field trace tier, deliberately. A two-tier design keeps every mesh's own distance field and, for a ray, culls the meshes near it into a froxel grid so the ray tests only those, finer than a coarse global field. This resamples every mesh field into the clipmap at build, culling the instances per cell as it goes, so the one global trace already carries the per-object detail such a tier would add — at the cost of the clipmap's own voxel resolution, which for indirect light is enough. A froxel-culled per-mesh tier would recover only sub-clipmap-voxel detail a bounce does not need, at the price of a second acceleration structure and a per-ray cull.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Presentation.Lighting.GlobalDistanceField.FloatsPerInstance

member.remarks: Everything is padded to vec4 even where three components would do. A std430 block packs a vec3 to a three-float stride on the CPU and a four-float alignment on the GPU, so a struct mixing the two reads correctly for its first element and slides for every one after it.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Presentation.Lighting.GlobalDistanceField.BuildLevel(System.Int32,OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3d)
member.summary: Sorts the level's objects into cells and dispatches the build for one clipmap level.
member.remarks: The culling grid is what makes this affordable. Without it every voxel consults every object, which for an outer level over a few hundred objects is hundreds of millions of transforms per rebuild; with it a voxel consults the handful that reach into its own cell.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Presentation.Lighting.GlobalDistanceField.RangeOf(System.Single)
member.summary: The furthest distance one clipmap level's bytes encode.
member.remarks:
A few voxels, not half the grid. The first version stored up to half the level's extent, which is wrong twice over. A grid cannot honour a distance far larger than its own resolution — it never recorded the detail that would justify one — and, more practically, a voxel that cares about geometry sixteen metres away needs every object within sixteen metres in its cull list, which on level 1 meant listing almost every object in almost every cell. That is what made the index buffer overflow.
Four voxels is what the nesting exists to permit: a ray that wants to step further than this steps in the next level out, whose voxels are twice as large and whose range is twice as far.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Presentation.Lighting.GlobalDistanceField.RangeOfLevel(System.Int32)
member.summary: The furthest distance a level's stored bytes encode.
member.param: The level, zero being the innermost.
member.returns: The range in metres.
member.remarks: Public so a pass tracing these clipmaps decodes them exactly as the build encoded them. Two copies of this number drifting apart would put every traced surface at the wrong distance.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Presentation.Lighting.GlobalLightSettings
member.summary: The level's own air and its flat light on models — the GlobalLight task and the keyframe it is showing.
member.param: The fog the ground is drawn into.
The fog models are drawn into.
The flat colour a model with no lightmap is multiplied by.
The keyframe's own time key, which is what selected it.

remarks.para: This is where the original's distance fog and its model lighting actually come from, and both were attributed to the wrong task at first: FlatSky's Fog Amount and Fog Color are the cloud plane's fade and the clear colour, not the air. sub_527520 — the GlobalLight update — finds the two GlobalLightKeyframe children bracketing the task's current time, interpolates all of their bands, and publishes the first two:

item.description: terrain → sub_50FE40 (0x50FE40) takes its ambient and sub_50FD20 (0x50FD20) its fog colour and its density × 0.0005 (0x527B41), which is what sub_512C30 fogs every terrain vertex with.
object category 1 → the model state block sub_49D480 reads its fog colour (flt_B818EC), its density (dword_B46D04) and its ambient (dword_B818AC).

remarks.para: The keyframes are not times of day. Every shipping level declares exactly two — 12, the mission's own air, and 100, which is green in all fourteen and carries no fog at all: the night-vision state. With the task's time at its start-up zero, sub_527520 finds no keyframe below it and copies the lowest one whole, so 12 is what a mission opens with.

The bands the levels ask for are far more varied than the one figure FlatSky suggested: half a surface gone by 71 m on the foggy third mission and by 2.9 km on the alpine eleventh, and a colour per level from warm sand to sky blue. That variety is the point — it is why mission 5's range is meant to be seen and mission 1's horizon is not.

remarks.para: L6's screen probe gather, the pass that finally carries the surface cache to the screen. Each probe reads its pixel's depth and normal from the G-buffer, rebuilds where that pixel sits in the world -- rebased onto this pass's origin so it lands in the same space the trace works in -- and gathers a hemisphere of rays through the shared software trace, reading the surface cache's final lighting at each hit. What comes back is the pixel's indirect irradiance, which a later pass interpolates across the probes and folds into the frame.

A probe grid rather than per pixel, because indirect light varies slowly and tracing every pixel would trace sixteen rays a pixel over the whole screen. Probes could be refined adaptively where depth or normal vary too fast for the grid to interpolate; that refinement is a later slice.

remarks.para: The same gather as the probes' -- the traced world first, then the cache's light where it struck, the sky or the open ground on a miss -- with a probe at every pixel and a single ray from it. The probes' own denoising, their pooling, cadence, accumulation and resolve, is exactly what ray reconstruction replaces, and handed their output it would see a smooth, lagging signal it was not trained on.

The screen comes first, as for the probes: a ray that lands on something in last frame's lit picture takes that light, read where the hit stood last frame. It is what carries a lamp's pool on the floor up onto the ceiling and a lit machine's glow onto the wall beside it, which the cards hold coarsely or not at all. Without it the interiors under ray reconstruction lost their bounce light.

member.remarks: L6c's temporal accumulation of the gather, with L5b's screen trace tier. The raw estimate is noisy -- sixteen jittered rays a frame -- so reading it straight ghosts and shimmers. Each probe reprojects its surface onto last frame's screen, reads the irradiance that accumulated there, and blends this frame's estimate in with a weight that falls as the frame count climbs, a running average. A reprojection that lands on a different surface, or off screen, drops the history rather than smearing it. Kept separate from the frame's own temporal anti-aliasing: this stabilises the gather in probe space before it is read, and the two filters compose.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Presentation.Lighting.SurfaceCacheCapture
member.summary: Renders every model into its cards' pages of the surface cache atlas, once, at load.

remarks.para: The point of the whole surface cache: after this runs, a ray that hits a model anywhere in the level can read what that surface looks like without the model being on screen, in the frustum, or drawn. Each card is one orthographic view, and the six of them together describe a model from any direction well enough to bounce light off.

Runs on the render thread and cannot move. Unlike the distance field bake, which is arithmetic, this is a render pass — the atlas is a framebuffer and the geometry is already uploaded, both of which belong to the context that made them.

Captured per model, not per placement. A level draws the same crate two hundred times and the crate looks the same every time, so its cards are captured once and every instance reads them. What an instance contributes is its transform, which the tracing side applies when it looks a card up.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Presentation.Lighting.SurfaceCacheInstances
member.summary: A lighting page for every placement of every card, and where each one stands in the world.

remarks.para: The split this type exists for. A card's surface is a property of the model: one crate looks like every other crate, so its albedo, normal and material are captured once and shared by all two hundred placements. A card's lighting is not: one crate stands in sunlight and another in the shadow of a hangar, and giving them the same page would light every crate in the level identically.

So there are two page layouts over the same cards. The captured one, from , has a page per model card. This one has a page per placement of each model card, and the lighting atlases are built to it. A texel of lighting finds its albedo at the same position within the card, in the other atlas.

The alternative — one per-instance atlas holding surface and lighting together — is simpler and costs the duplication of every model's albedo once per placement. On level 1 that is 687 copies of 106 models' surfaces, about six and a half times the memory, for data that is identical in every copy.
