member.name: T:OpenIGI.Presentation.Lighting.SurfaceCacheLighting
member.summary: Lights every card page, so that a ray hitting a surface reads light rather than albedo.

remarks.para: The captured pages hold unlit albedo — see CardAtlasShaders for why a shared card cannot carry a placement's bake. This pass is what puts light into the cache: for every texel of every placement's pages it works out where that surface stands in the world, what direction it faces, and what reaches it.

The reconstruction is the whole difficulty. A lighting texel knows only its position in an atlas. Getting back to a world position means: which page, therefore which card and which placement; where in the card's rectangle; how far behind the card's plane the surface sits; and then through the placement's transform. Every step of that can be subtly wrong in a way that still produces lit surfaces — just in the wrong places — which looks like nothing at all until a later stage bounces light off them.

Work is dispatched per tile, not per page. Pages vary in size, so one dispatch each would be thousands of dispatches; one dispatch over the whole atlas would have every invocation search for its page. Instead the pages are cut into fixed tiles once, on the CPU, and a work group takes one tile — so an invocation knows its page from its group and the atlas's empty space costs nothing.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Presentation.Lighting.SurfaceCacheLighting.TemporalFrames
member.summary: Gets or sets how many frames the temporal accumulation converges over.
member.remarks:
The cap on the accumulation weight: the blend's alpha bottoms out at one over this, so the estimate keeps adapting to a moving sun or a shifting shadow rather than freezing, while still integrating far more hemisphere directions than the sixteen a single frame traces.
This is the knob for the slow travelling ripple over interior surfaces -- the "heat haze" visible with the camera standing perfectly still. See r_gi_temporal_frames, which owns the reasoning and the measurements; settable here, like , so the trade between a steady still and a responsive scrubbed sun can be dialled without a rebuild. The default is the value the constant held before the cvar existed, so a caller that never sets it is unchanged.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Presentation.Lighting.SurfaceCacheLighting.BounceFrameSpread
member.summary: How many frames a steady-state bounce spreads the cache's tiles across.
member.remarks:
The per-frame relight traces the whole surface cache against the distance field, which on a large level is the single most expensive pass in the frame -- measured at twenty-six milliseconds on mission 1, a frame all by itself. The geometry and the sun are static, so a tile re-traced this frame gives the same answer it would several frames from now: dividing the cache into this many slices and advancing one slice a frame cuts the per-frame cost by the same factor while a still scene still reaches the same equilibrium, only a few frames later. The temporal blend already carries a tile's estimate between its updates, so the seam between an updated slice and a stale one is not visible. The seed pass on a clipmap rebuild still relights every tile at once.
Twelve, not six. This stage is world-space -- its cost is the same at any output resolution -- so on a slower GPU or a high-resolution frame it is the single biggest item in the budget (twelve milliseconds at 1440p on one machine); halving the per-frame slice roughly halves it. A converged still is identical either way (measured: 0.7% mean pixel difference against a six-slice frame); the only cost is that a tile the camera newly reveals reaches its multi-bounce answer over twelve frames rather than six -- a fifth of a second longer at sixty, under the temporal blend that hides the seam.
Settable, not a constant, so the trade -- per-frame GPU cost against how quickly a newly revealed surface fills in -- can be dialled from a cvar without a rebuild. Higher is cheaper and lags more.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Presentation.Lighting.SurfaceCacheLighting.ActiveCentre
member.summary: Where the steady-state refresh is centred, relative to this cache's own origin.
member.remarks: The camera, in practice. Meaningless unless is positive.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Presentation.Lighting.SurfaceCacheLighting.ActiveRadius
member.summary: How far from the steady-state refresh reaches, in metres.

remarks.para: Nought relights the whole level, which is what the load-time seed and the deterministic dump want and what every frame used to do. A positive radius is the steady-state case: the cursor still walks every tile, but a tile whose card lies beyond this returns before it reads a texel.

Why the whole level was ever wrong. These maps are kilometres across and a player stands in a corner of one, so the great majority of the cache is somewhere they cannot see. Worse, the distance field the relight traces against is a clipmap that follows the camera and reaches a few hundred metres — beyond it there is no geometry to trace, so a far tile's relight cannot even produce a different answer from the one it already holds. It was spending real milliseconds recomputing what it had.

Far cards are not left dark: the load-time seed lights the whole cache once with no radius, and they keep that until the camera brings them back inside. What they lose is only the tracking of changes — a lamp switched two hundred metres away does not relight the wall beside it until the player walks over, which is the trade this exists to make.

remarks.para: A truck that drives off with the camera inside it: its cards were captured in the model's own space and their records placed them where it stood at load. Unmoved, every ray that struck its interior looked the surface up where the truck USED to be and read a wall of the yard, or nothing -- the GI inside went dark and smeared. Rewritten here, the lookup finds the truck's own surface wherever it is.

The first move also takes the pages out of the static lookup grid, which still files them at the load-time spot, and into the short list of movers every lookup walks. And it stops them being relit: the shadows the lighting traces come from a distance field built from the level as it loaded, in which this object still stands where it started, so lighting it at its new place would light it as if it were not there. Its pages carry the light they had, as the surface carries its colour.
Uploaded once a frame, by .

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Presentation.Lighting.SurfaceCacheLighting.DeferredLampScale
member.summary: What a fixture's relative intensity is worth, as the deferred lamps weigh it.

remarks.para: The SAME light the screen shows, because this is what the room's bounce is integrated from. The deferred pass gives a lamp pi * r_local_light_scale * min(intensity, 1.5) / (d^2 + 1) of irradiance (its Lambert albedo/pi times the kPi on its lamp term). This used to be a constant 0.35 picked by eye with neither the pi nor the preset's scale -- at ultra some fifty times less lamp light in the cache than on screen, so a lamp-lit floor bounced next to nothing onto the ceiling above it and every interior's ceiling read black at night.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Presentation.Lighting.SurfaceCacheLighting.Bounce(OpenIGI.Presentation.Lighting.GlobalDistanceField,System.Single,System.Int32,System.Int32)
member.summary: Gathers the bounce, then folds it into the atlas a trace should read.
member.param: The clipmaps to trace against. Without them there is nothing to gather.

The albedo boost the surface's diffuse colour is passed through before it reflects light on. Clamped below one inside the shader, which is what stops the feedback running away: a surface that returned everything it received, every iteration, would diverge.

How many times to bounce on the first pass. Each one reads the last one's answer, so two iterations is light that has reflected twice, and the cost is linear while the benefit falls off quickly. Only used on the first pass; the steady state gathers once and lets the further bounce arrive over frames.

Which frame of the accumulation this is. Zero is a one-shot with no history -- the load pass and every dump -- and stays deterministic; above it the gather jitters its hemisphere per frame and blends onto what each probe already held, so the estimate integrates far more directions than one frame's sixteen and settles as the count rises.
member.remarks: The first pass converges in one shot; the steady state accumulates. On the first pass the final atlas is seeded with the direct term's outgoing radiance and then gathered and combined times, so a still scene is lit without waiting for frames. Once running, each relight gathers once -- reading last frame's final, so a further bounce arrives over frames -- blends the result onto the running estimate, and folds it back into the final. It does not re-seed, because that would throw away the bounce the final already carries. The gather cannot read and write one atlas at once -- invocations run in no known order -- which is what forces the split into separate dispatches, and is also what keeps the last answer around for the next to build on.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Presentation.Lighting.SurfaceCacheLighting.DefaultBoost
member.summary: The albedo boost a surface's diffuse colour is passed through by default.
member.remarks: A diffuse colour boost. Below one it raises a dark surface's albedo towards but never to one, so light bouncing between dim interior surfaces does not vanish; at one or above it is identity. This is the single knob that decides whether interiors read as lit or as washed out, and it is the first thing to reach for. The clamp below one in the shader is also what keeps the multi-bounce feedback from diverging.

remarks.para: Without ray tracing, whether a lamp reaches a texel of the cache was asked of the distance field alone. member.name: M:OpenIGI.Presentation.Lighting.SurfaceCacheLighting.SetLocalLightLevels(OpenIGI.Game.World.LampSwitchboard)
member.summary: Re-sends the same lights at whatever output a switchboard says they are giving out.
member.param: The level's lamps, indexed as the fixtures were.

remarks.para: The bounce has to follow the switch or a switched-off lamp goes on filling the room with indirect light out of a fitting that is visibly dark — the one artefact that would give the whole thing away, because it is exactly the light the player switched off, arriving one bounce later.

An overwrite rather than a rebuild: destroys and recreates the buffer, which is a per-level cost and not one to pay while a tube is stuttering. Only the strength is rewritten — position, reach and facing are properties of the fitting and a switch does not move it — so this is one upload of a few kilobytes over a buffer that is already the right shape.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Presentation.Lighting.SurfaceCacheLookup
member.summary: Finds which card page covers a point in the world, so that a ray which hits a surface can read what that surface is lit by.

remarks.para: This is what makes a traced bounce possible. Sphere tracing against the distance field answers "how far to the nearest surface" and nothing else — it returns a distance, not a thing. A ray that stops somewhere therefore knows it hit, but not what it hit, and a bounce needs the radiance leaving whatever was struck. The surface cache holds that radiance per card page; this is the index that gets from a world position to the right page of it.

A uniform grid, because the pages never move. A level's geometry is static, so the structure is built once at load and never rebuilt — which rules out the usual objection to uniform grids, that they are expensive to keep current. What is left is their one real advantage: a constant-time lookup with no traversal, which matters when every ray of every probe does one.

Its cells are hashed rather than laid out in a box, which is what lets the cell be a fixed eight metres whatever the level is shaped like. A box grid has to divide the level's own extent, so its cell is decided by the geometry furthest out — and a mission is not one compact box: level 8 is three bases with open ground between them, and most missions leave a handful of props parked kilometres away from all of it. See for what that cost.

Cells hold page indices rather than placements. A placement's pages face different ways and sit in different parts of its bounding box, so going through the placement would mean testing every card of a large object to find the one facing the ray — whereas a page's own bounds are tight enough that the grid does most of the rejecting.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Presentation.Lighting.SurfaceCacheLookup.Buckets
member.summary: How many buckets the grid's cells are hashed into.
member.remarks: Two million, which is sixteen megabytes of ranges, built once and never rebuilt — the same table the grid had when it was a hundred and twenty-eight cells cubed and addressed directly. A power of two, so the hash is masked rather than divided.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Presentation.Lighting.SurfaceCacheLookup.CellMetres
member.summary: How large one cell is, in metres, on every axis of every level.

remarks.para: Fixed, which is the whole point. The cell used to be the level's longest span divided by a hundred and twenty-eight, so a level's own shape decided how finely it was indexed — and what actually decided it was the geometry FURTHEST from the level. Level 4 leaves twenty-seven objects at the world origin, thirty kilometres from the base; level 1 keeps twenty-seven buildings three kilometres underground; level 8 keeps a room of props a hundred kilometres straight up. Level 8 is also the first mission built as three separate bases with open ground between them, so its span was large before the strays even counted. Measured to those, its cell came out at 795 metres: the entire playable level fell into six cells of the two million, and the busiest held 4932 of the 6042 page references. A lookup walks its cell, so every ray that hit anything walked most of the level — 29 ms a frame of global illumination on level 8 against 4 ms on level 1, whose cache is only a third smaller. That was the one mission-specific frame-rate cliff in the game.

Hashing the cells instead of laying them out in a box is what lets the size be fixed: a level can be any size, in any number of pieces, anywhere, and the cost of a lookup follows how densely the geometry is packed rather than how far apart its far corners are. Nothing has to be judged as belonging to the level or not, which matters for a game whose missions really do have several bases kilometres apart.

Eight metres because that is the scale of what a card is: a wall, a hut, a container. Measured across the fourteen missions it leaves the busiest bucket between 60 and 250 pages, where the spread used to run from 72 to 4932.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Presentation.Lighting.SurfaceCacheLookup.MaximumCellsPerPage
member.summary: The most cells one card page may be filed under before it is left out as malformed.
member.remarks: Forty cells cubed, or a card three hundred metres across. The widest card in the retail missions reaches a hundred and twenty-two metres from its model's origin, so this leaves about a factor of two in hand. It exists because hashing removed the bound the box grid used to impose for free.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Presentation.Lighting.SurfaceCacheLookup.MaximumMoverPages
member.summary: How many pages of moving placements the lookup can list.
member.remarks: The movers' list is one more bucket after the hashed ones -- index -- which every lookup consults as well as its own cell. A page that moves cannot be filed by where it is: the grid is built once. A truck is a few dozen pages; this is room for a level's worth of vehicles, doors and lifts, and the buffer is sized for it up front so its handle never changes.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Presentation.Lighting.SurfaceCacheLookup.MaximumMoverObjects
member.summary: How many moving placements the lookup can list.
member.remarks: The movers' bucket lists objects, each with a bounding sphere and the run of its pages, so a lookup tests one sphere per object and walks only the pages of those it falls within. Walking every mover's page from every lookup was half the cost of every traced bounce on level 3, whose vehicles and doors come to two hundred and sixty pages.

member.summary: How many ints one object's entry in the movers' list takes; matches the shader's kMoverHeaderInts.
member.remarks: Its bounding sphere's centre and radius as float bits, then its pages' start and count.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Presentation.Lighting.SurfaceCacheLookup.Bucket(System.Int32,System.Int32,System.Int32)
member.summary: Which bucket a cell is filed under. Must match the shader's hash exactly.
member.remarks: Teschner's three large primes, one per axis, exclusive-ored and masked down to the table. Chosen because it is short enough to be written twice -- once here and once in GLSL -- with no doubt that the two agree, which is the only property that matters: a page filed under a bucket the lookup does not compute is a page the bounce cannot find. Unsigned multiplication wraps identically in both languages, and a negative index converts to the same bit pattern in both.

member.remarks: Given the baked field's own layout so the two are interchangeable at the sampler: the deferred pass reads whichever volume the device binds with the same origin, spacing and counts. A re-configure with the identical layout is a no-op -- the cache keeps accumulating rather than starting cold -- so this is safe to call every frame from the game layer without resetting the field each time.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Presentation.Lighting.SurfaceCacheRadianceVolume.UpdateRadianceCache(OpenIGI.Presentation.Lighting.GlobalDistanceField,OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3f,System.Int32,System.Single,System.Single)
member.summary: Traces one amortised slab of the radiance cache against the surface cache and the sky.
member.param: The clipmaps to trace against; without them there is nothing to gather.
The radiance a ray that escapes the geometry carries.
The ceiling on the running average, so the field keeps adapting rather than freezing.
A calibration factor on the stored radiance, to dial the bounce into the tuned range.
The escape fraction under which a probe's sky reads as a wall leak and is dropped.
member.remarks: Each probe fires a sphere of rays through the shared software trace, reads the surface cache's final lighting at each hit and the sky where a ray escapes, projects the result into first-order harmonics -- the exact scale the baked stores, so the two read back identically -- and blends it onto the probe's running estimate. Because the estimate lives in a world cell rather than a screen probe, it does not move with the camera and does not need reprojection: that is the whole reason it is stable where the screen gather is not. Only a slab is traced each frame; the first full sweep overwrites the freshly allocated garbage, and every sweep after it blends.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Presentation.Lighting.SurfaceCacheRelight
member.summary: The card relight: the one program that lights every page directly, gathers its bounce and folds the two into the atlas a trace reads, dispatched a tile per work group over the whole cache, a slice of it, or the compacted list of tiles near the camera.
member.remarks: Owns the program, the tile cursors that spread the steady state over frames, and the active tile list. exposes it and decides when each pass runs.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Presentation.Lighting.SurfaceCacheRelight.ActiveRebuildMargin
member.summary: How far the camera may drift from where the active list was built before a rebuild.
member.remarks: The list is built against plus this, so every page the shader's exact test could accept stays on the list until the centre has moved further than the slack -- the superset guarantee that makes the list invisible in the image.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Presentation.Lighting.SurfaceCacheRelight.MinSliceGroups
member.summary: The fewest tiles a steady-state slice dispatches, when there is more than a slice left.
member.remarks:
An even split of the active list can be a very small dispatch -- a few hundred work groups at an outdoor spawn -- and this shader's cost is ray latency, which a small dispatch cannot hide: per tile it measured about four times slower at four hundred groups than at three thousand. So a slice is never smaller than this; when the active list is short, the round finishes its coverage in the first few frames at full occupancy and the remaining frames dispatch nothing at all, rather than every frame paying the latency of an underfilled machine. Refresh cadence is unchanged either way: one full pass over the active set per .
1024 rather than the 4096 it was: at 4096 a round's bounce landed on a handful of frames at up to 6.5 ms each at 1440p ultra and idled the rest, which was the largest single cause of the 1% low. At 1024 the peak is about 2 ms for some 0.2 ms more on average; at 512 the latency cost began to show in the average (the bounce doubled). The image is the same at any value.

member.remarks: Interleaved rather than contiguous, with set to the slice count by the caller: tiles are laid out page by page, so a contiguous slice is one part of the level, and its cost was that part's -- a slice over a dense interior took several times the frame time of one over open ground, which is a spike once every sweep. member.name: T:OpenIGI.Presentation.FixedFunctionSun
member.summary: The one light a title's fixed-function pipeline shone on an object that had no baked lightmap: a flat ambient plus one directional colour, evaluated per vertex.

remarks.para: I.G.I. 2 draws an unlightmapped object with D3DRS_LIGHTING = 1 and a white material (Direct3DRender_SetGenericStateRigid, igi2ed 0x56CA90), its stage 0 set to MODULATE(TEXTURE, DIFFUSE) (Direct3DRender_SetTextureStateRigid, 0x56CE10), so the whole of its lighting is what Direct3D's vertex pipeline puts in DIFFUSE: the global ambient plus each enabled light's diffuse times the cosine of its angle to the vertex normal, saturated to one. The level supplies exactly one such light — a D3DLIGHT_DIRECTIONAL whose diffuse is the Dirlight keyframe's front colour and whose direction is the negated sun vector (Direct3DRender_AddLightsource, 0x56C750) — and the ambient is the GlobalLight keyframe's first object category (GlobalLightQTask_DrawCallback, 0x6534E0, through Lightsource_SetAmbientlight, 0x41C990).

So a vertex facing the sun is lit saturate(Ambient + Colour) and one facing away is lit Ambient, and a title that authors night by colouring the sun dark, as the sequel does, gets dark objects out of it. A port that draws those objects at their texture alone draws them in full daylight.

member.param: The flat light every unlightmapped vertex receives, linear.
The directional light's diffuse colour, linear.
The unit vector towards the light, in world space.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Presentation.ObjectShading
member.summary: How a title composites the objects its world pass draws.

remarks.para: A title seam about compositing, kept apart from the one about air. says what colour the distance goes; this says how a baked lightmap is applied and what lights an object that has none. They are read off the same level but they reach different places — the atmosphere is baked into every pipeline, this is applied per draw — and a change to one has no business reaching the other.

is the port's long-standing behaviour: a lightmap multiplies at one and an unlightmapped object is drawn unshaded. Project I.G.I. answers nothing at the seam and gets exactly that, which is how its picture is left alone.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Presentation.Rendering.BinocularOptics
member.summary: The render-side fade that raises and lowers the remastered binocular's glass lens transform.

remarks.para: Title-agnostic, which is why it sits here rather than beside one game's renderers: it is a clamped ramp over a wall-clock delta whose only other type comes from , and both games have binoculars — I.G.I. 2's levels name OVERLAY_BINOCULAR in their own scripts.

This is presentation state, deliberately kept off the simulation. BinocularsView owns whether the device is open, but it ticks on the fixed 30 Hz clock and exposes only edges, not a continuous envelope. The glass is a display transform applied at resolve time, so its fade has to run on the render/wall clock -- otherwise it would advance in 30 Hz steps and shimmer, and would fade faster on a faster machine. This mirrors MapComputerCamera.DisplayAmount, which raises the map tube the same way.
The close is a little quicker than the open: lowering the binoculars is a deliberate action and a lingering lens reads as lag, whereas the raise wants a moment of the glass settling in.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Presentation.Rendering.BitmapTextRenderer
member.summary: Lays out and draws strings with a bitmap font.

remarks.para: Layout follows the original's font object (Font_Create, 0x4B6DB0): a cursor, a per-axis scale and a colour. Each character resolves through the font's TRAN map to a glyph, the glyph is drawn at the cursor plus its own offset, and the cursor advances by the glyph's advance.

The original's sprite and text colours are on a scale of 128: it initialises a font's colour to 128.0f and multiplies every colour by 1/128 on its way to the vertex (0x534AB0), so 128 is the art as it is. The 2D batch multiplies by the colour as a fraction of 255, so is full white and converts the original's colours.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Presentation.Rendering.DayNightCycle
member.summary: An interactive day/night cycle: the level's authored sun, swept across the sky by a time of day the player scrubs with two keys, and re-orientable on every axis.

remarks.para: The level ships one authored sun, at noon. This treats that as the arc's high point and rotates it down towards each horizon and under the world as the time of day moves away from noon, so a single static direction becomes a full sunrise-to-night sweep. At the authored hour with no re-orientation the result reproduces the authored sun exactly, so the cycle sitting in the pipeline changes nothing until a key is pressed.

It exists to be driven live, which is what the real-time radiance cache was built for: every step of the sun re-lights the surface cache and the cache re-gathers it, so the bounce, the shadows and the sky fill all follow the sun round without a re-bake.
It also runs on its own, when the player has asked it to, at a day length they set: that is the ordinary day/night cycle rather than the scrub, and it arrives through .

Controls (ignored while the console has the keyboard): [ and ] scrub the time of day -- held, a full day passes in seconds; the numpad re-orients the arc, 4/6 around world Z, 8/2 around X, 9/7 around Y, and 5 clears the re-orientation and returns to noon.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Presentation.Rendering.DayNightCycle.SecondsPerDay
member.summary: Real seconds a held scrub key takes to advance a whole day.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Presentation.Rendering.DayNightCycle.AutomaticTicksPerDay
member.summary: How many times the automatic cycle moves the clock over one whole day.

remarks.para: The clock is advanced in whole ticks rather than continuously, and this is why: the sun is the most expensive thing in the frame to move. Every distinct direction re-lights the surface cache, re-gathers the radiance cache and re-fits the shadow cascades, and a sun advanced by a sliver on every frame is a sun that never repeats -- so all of that runs perpetually, for a change nobody can see. Held still between ticks, the sweep hands its consumers the same direction for a stretch of frames and they can tell that nothing moved.

Counted per DAY rather than fixed in seconds so that a tick is always the same slice of the arc -- a tenth of a degree of sun -- whatever a day has been set to cost in real time. That is what lets the day length be a variable at all: at forty minutes a day the clock ticks about every two-thirds of a second, at an hour once a second, at a minute every frame, and the sweep is equally smooth at all of them. A tick fixed in seconds would instead be a step of sky that grew with the rate, and past a point that is a sun which visibly jumps.
The scrub keys deliberately do NOT tick -- they sweep a day in and are meant to be held and watched.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Presentation.Rendering.DayNightCycle.DefaultNightColour
member.summary: What the moon carries when the level does not say: about an eightieth of a sun, cool.

remarks.para: This is the cycle's own invention, and it stands for every level that authors no night of its own -- which is all of Project I.G.I.

Not the physical ratio, on purpose. A full moon is some four hundred thousand times dimmer than the sun, about nineteen stops. No display and no eye adaptation this game models spans that, and shown at the true ratio a night is simply black. Games and film show a night a few stops under day and carry the rest of "night" in colour: a cool key, a blue sky, and the resolve's Purkinje shift taking the colour out of what the moon lights. It was three-thousandths of a sun; with an exposure that also fell by more than a stop at night, a night mission's ground came out nearly six times darker than the original draws it. A fortieth, with the night sky and airglow filling the shadows, lit the world as a floodlit yard; at an eightieth it reads as moonlight, and r_moonlight scales it from there.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Presentation.Rendering.DayNightCycle.Nightfall
member.summary: Gets how far into night the sun has gone: nought in daylight, one under a midnight sky.
member.remarks: Measured off the sun's own elevation before the moon takes its place, and eased across a band that opens as the sun reaches the horizon and closes once it is properly under it -- so it comes on through dusk and goes off through dawn rather than switching at a moment. What reads it is the exposure: the frame is shown a little darker at night, because the eye adaptation otherwise spends the night lifting it back towards day. Stays nought when is bypassed.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Presentation.Rendering.DayNightCycle.MoonDirection
member.summary: Gets the world direction towards the moon, whether or not it is up.
member.remarks: The arc's anti-solar point, which is where the cycle hangs its moon -- always full, because it always stands opposite the sun. Reported even while the sun holds the directional slot, so the sky can draw a rising moon through dusk before its light takes over. Straight down when is bypassed.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Presentation.Rendering.DayNightCycle.StarVisibility
member.summary: Gets how visible the stars are: nought in daylight, one once the sun is well under.
member.remarks: The eye picks out the first stars at nautical twilight and the full field only at astronomical twilight, the sun six and eighteen degrees under. The band follows that, in the sine of the sun's elevation, so the stars come out through dusk and fade through dawn. Stays nought when is bypassed.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Presentation.Rendering.DayNightCycle.SunDirection
member.summary: Gets the world direction towards the sun, wherever it is -- under the horizon included.
member.remarks: Unlike , never the moon's. The sky keeps scattering the sun from here after the moon has taken the direct light: that is the twilight glow, which fades as the sun sinks rather than going out when the direct light changes hands. Straight up when is bypassed.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Presentation.Rendering.DayNightCycle.SkySunColour
member.summary: Gets the sun's light before the air has coloured it, for the sky to scatter.
member.remarks: The level's authored sun, untinted and at full strength whatever the hour. The sky's own march reddens and dims it on the way through, and the planet's shadow puts it out; a sun already reddened and dimmed here would be reddened a second time -- which is what turned every direction of a sunset sky orange-brown -- and would take the twilight glow down with the direct light.

member.remarks: Reported whether or not it holds the direct light, so the sky can scatter it as a second source from the moment it clears the horizon rather than only once it outshines the setting sun.

remarks.para: The cycle invents a night because a level that authors its sun at noon does not have one. A level that DOES author one -- I.G.I. 2's night missions, which paint the sun nearly black and leave it up -- is bound to the cycle by that end instead, and then the invented night is the wrong night: it is about thirty times darker in the directional and half as bright in the fill, so the mission would open far darker than its artists drew it.
Set per level and cleared by , so a level that says nothing cannot inherit the last one's night. Project I.G.I. never says anything and keeps the constants it always had.

Nought or less stops it -- which is what the caller passes wherever time should not be passing, a menu or a paused mission -- and drops the seconds banked towards the next tick, so a pause never releases a jump. member.summary: Splits a collision triangle using the distance-aware, longest-edge recursion in native FUN_0044A670. The retail routine measures the contact against every edge, converts that distance with 1/5120, and keeps splitting while any edge exceeds 409.6 + 4505.6 * normalizedDistance engine units. Its split point is deliberately not a midpoint: the short/long edge ratio is clamped around 0.5 and offset by the retail random range of 0.1. Keeping the recursion order is important because the native 999-record cap is an insertion-order cap.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Presentation.Rendering.ImpactParticleRenderer
member.summary: Simulates and draws the particle bursts where rounds land.

remarks.para: Presentation only, and optional (r_impact_particles; the vanilla preset pins it to zero). Each burst is composed from what the material table says was struck: sparks are additive velocity-stretched streaks that fall under real gravity and die fast; dust is alpha-blended soft billboards that drift off the surface, expand and thin out. Particles step on the fixed 30 Hz tick like everything else and are drawn interpolated between ticks, so they glide at any frame rate without the simulation owing anything to it.

Every rule the tracer renderer learned the hard way is followed here: geometry streams through one fixed-capacity mesh updated in place (never create-and-draw in the same frame), draws happen in the FORWARD pass with the emissive override (light must not land in the G-buffer), the procedural textures shape their alpha (a solid-alpha quad stamps rectangles into the scene's alpha channel), every epsilon guard rejects NaN by polarity, and each emitted quad is finite-checked — a NaN reaching the HDR target is the one thing an additive blend can darken with.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Presentation.Rendering.InteractionBadgeSprite
member.summary: The interaction marker's key badge, generated once as a small antialiased sprite.

remarks.para: Why it is baked rather than drawn. The painter has no antialiased line and no blur, so a badge assembled at draw time is a stack of filled shapes, each covering the middle of the one before it. That composes correctly only at full opacity: the marker fades in and out, every layer's alpha is scaled by the fade, and a face that no longer covers what is under it leaves the rim showing through as a lighter middle — with a hard seam wherever the light along the top was clipped. Baked, the whole badge is one image with one alpha, so the fade multiplies it uniformly and the figure is identical at every opacity.
It also buys the light. The rim brightens towards the top by the angle of each texel rather than by clipping bands across the shape, which is a gradient no combination of filled rectangles can draw.

Two quadrants are stored, not one: the badge is symmetrical left to right but not top to bottom, so the upper half is mirrored horizontally into two corners and the lower half into the other two. A key cap stretches the column through each quadrant's inner edge across its straight middle, exactly as does — that column is the shape's vertical profile and is constant along a straight edge.

member.remarks: The dark separation edge lives outside the rim, so the drawn figure is wider than the badge the caller asks for. Callers size the rim and this converts.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Presentation.Rendering.InteractionBadgeSprite.Quadrant
member.summary: The quadrant's size in texels.
member.remarks: Forty-eight carries the rim and the light inside it cleanly at the sizes a badge is drawn — a little over 40 pixels across at 1080p and about twice that at 4K — and the atlas is 32 KB.

member.summary: The prompt's own wall clock: which offer is on screen, how far it has faded up, and how far its entry pop has run.

remarks.para: State the renderer must not own, for the reason BinocularOptics does not: the fade is measured in real seconds so it runs at the same rate at any frame rate, and it has to survive the frames when nothing is offered at all — otherwise the marker vanishes the instant the player's aim leaves the door instead of falling away from it.

member.remarks: A verdict is read back once the slot's fence comes round, so the culler skips a page a frame or two after the depth that judged it was written. Standing still that is exactly right. Turning is a statement about where the camera was looking, not where it is: a page that has just come out from behind a hill still carries the verdict it earned while hidden, so it is skipped -- the hole -- until its retest lands and it is drawn again.
member.param: Whether sustained travel is also judged over a window of frames (see ), as well as each frame's own step.

member.summary: How far the camera may drift per frame and still count as holding still, in metres.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Presentation.Rendering.OcclusionSettle.SettleOrientation
member.summary: How far any orientation element may move per frame and still count as holding still.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Presentation.Rendering.OcclusionSettle.WindowFrames
member.summary: How many frames the cumulative-movement window spans.
member.remarks: The per-frame is fooled by a HIGH FRAME RATE and by a SLOW CINEMATIC PAN: sustained travel whose every step is under the per-frame threshold reads as "still" frame after frame, so occlusion re-engages while the camera is in fact moving, and terrain emerging from behind a hill is culled on the stale "occluded" verdict it earned while hidden -- the black flash on a mission switch and during fast flight. Judging the camera against where it was a whole window ago catches that travel however it is paced, because occlusion depends on camera POSITION (a hill either hides a point or it does not), never on where the camera looks -- so a windowed position test is both sufficient and exact.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Presentation.Rendering.OcclusionSettle.WindowDistance

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Presentation.Rendering.Particle2DRenderer
member.summary: Draws the 2-D particle engine both titles share (): every live particle as its system's sprite, as Particle2DDynCubeObj_EnterHandler (Project I.G.I. 0x4FD020) draws it.

remarks.para: A particle is a camera-facing quad, its half-extents the system's width and height, times the particle's size where the system grows; turned by its rotation where it spins; of its frame where the sprite is animated. Nothing inside half a metre of the eye, nor past the system's range, is drawn, and a quad's projected half is never under half a pixel.

The colour is the system's, on the sprite renderer's scale where 128 is white. A system that fades by opacity () draws its particles at their intensity's alpha; one that does not darkens their colour by it at full alpha. The blend is the graphic flags': additive, darkening and multiplying sprites as such, everything else an ordinary alpha blend. A shiny system takes the world's light into its colour in the original; none of either title's systems is shiny, so the system's own colour is drawn.

The sprites are the title's own, from the common sprite archive both titles ship. The quads are drawn emissive, over the lit scene, divided by the scene's exposure as the first-person rig is -- without it a dark scene's adaptation clipped the blood's red while it lifted the rest, and the spray came out pink. A particle is drawn between its last two ticks: the step is a plain Euler one, so a tick ago it stood one speed back.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Presentation.Rendering.PrecipitationGeometry.SphereAverageCosine
member.summary: The light a particle is seen by: the frame's sky fill, desaturated and scaled.

remarks.para: One frame's worth, so it is computed once and handed to every particle rather than recomputed per quad. What it stands in for, and why it is not the frame itself, is in the type's own remarks.

It multiplies the particle's colour; it is not added to it. Adding a desaturated tap of the light behind a drop to its emissive while also lighting its base colour comes out, over alpha blending, very close to simply adding the lit colour, because the ambient term all but cancels the attenuation the blend applies. So the drops are drawn additively and carry the lit colour, which is one multiply instead of two terms and a blend, and lands in the same place.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Presentation.Rendering.PrecipitationSimulation.StepWind(System.Single,OpenIGI.Rendering.PrecipitationSettings)
member.summary: Wanders the wind towards a new speed and heading, and returns where it is now.

remarks.para: A target inside the settings' range, eased towards, and replaced before it is reached. What that gives is rain whose lean is never quite the same twice and never changes abruptly either — the two things a single fixed wind speed cannot do. A step change would be worse than no wind at all: the whole column shears in one frame, which reads as the camera being knocked rather than as air.

The easing is per second and independent of the target, so an unusually large change takes proportionally longer rather than snapping — and the hold before the next target is itself randomised, so the wind has no period for the eye to lock onto.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Presentation.Rendering.PrecipitationSimulation.Noise(System.Single,System.Single,System.Single)
member.summary: A cheap deterministic hash of a lattice point, which is built from.

remarks.para: Internal so the gust shape can be asserted on directly: a field that is accidentally constant makes the storm look even rather than broken, which is not a difference anyone spots by eye.

Integers, not a sine. This was the usual frac(sin(dot(p, k)) * 43758), which costs a transcendental. Twelve thousand drops each taking two smoothed samples is a hundred and ninety thousand sines a frame, which is milliseconds of CPU spent on a field nobody can point at — and the sine's own periodicity puts visible structure in it at large coordinates, where the world actually is. A bit mix is a handful of integer operations and better distributed.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Presentation.Rendering.PrecipitationSimulation.SmoothNoise(System.Single,System.Single,System.Single)
member.summary: A smooth value noise in [0, 1]: the hash on a unit lattice, interpolated between.

remarks.para: Why this exists at all. The gust field was the raw hash, sampled at the drop's own position. A hash has no correlation length: two drops a hand's breadth apart get unrelated values, so what was meant to arrive as sheets of rain came out as per-drop random opacity — invisible as sheets, and visible as the storm having a slightly dirty, speckled quality. A gust field has to be smooth: neighbouring drops must agree, or there is no sheet.

The same is true of the glimmer for a different reason. Sampled from a hash on a coordinate that moves with time, a drop's flash is a fresh random number every frame — a strobe rather than a glint. Interpolated, it ramps up and back down over the several frames it takes the coordinate to cross a lattice cell, which is what a drop catching the light actually does.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Presentation.Rendering.PrecipitationSimulation.SpawnDrift(System.Single,System.Single,System.Single,System.Single)
member.summary: The acceleration the air gives a drop, in metres per second squared.
member.param: The strongest push the air may give, from the settings.
A random number, zero to one, for how hard this drop is pushed.
A random number, zero to one, for its compass direction.
A random number, zero to one, for how far above or below level.
member.returns: The acceleration on all three axes.

remarks.para: Three dimensions, not two. A push confined to the horizontal plane leaves the fall looking the same from above as from the side, and every drop's streak the same length: the whole variety of it then lives in one plane, which is exactly what "it looks the same at every viewing angle" describes. Air moves up and down as well as along.

A direction and a magnitude rather than a number per axis, and the direction is even over the SPHERE — the elevation is drawn as a cosine rather than as an angle, because drawing the angle evenly crowds the poles. The magnitude takes a cube root so that the magnitudes fill the ball's VOLUME evenly instead of crowding its middle.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Presentation.Rendering.PrecipitationSimulation.DriftAt(System.Single,System.Single,System.Single,System.Single,System.Single)
member.summary: The sideways velocity a drop has drifted to by a given age, in metres per second.
member.param: The wind the drop was born in, east.
The wind the drop was born in, north.
The drop's own acceleration, east.
The drop's own acceleration, north.
How long it has been falling.
member.returns: The horizontal velocity.
member.remarks: The wind is the same for every drop born at that moment and the drift is the drop's own, so what separates two streaks is how long each has been falling. This is why the fall shows a range of angles at all: it is a population of ages, not a population of velocities.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Presentation.Rendering.PrecipitationSimulation.TerminalFor(System.Single,System.Single)
member.summary: How fast a drop of a given size settles to falling, in metres per second.
member.param: The settings' fall speed, which the largest drop reaches.
The drop's size, from the smallest share up to one.
member.returns: The speed, never below half a metre a second.
member.remarks: Straight-line in size: the largest drop falls at the full speed and the smallest at half of it. Small drops falling slower is what lets one sideways push lean them further than the big ones, which is a good part of why the column does not read as parallel lines.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Presentation.Rendering.PrecipitationSpriteSheets
member.summary: Composes and uploads the storm's sprite sheets: the stacked drop strips, the channel-unpacked splash animations with the droplet blob, and the far sheets' cloud.
member.remarks: Each sheet is read from the executable's weather assets and falls back on a generated stand-in at the same layout, so every index the storm addresses still means what it means.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Presentation.Rendering.PrecipitationSpriteSheets.BuildDropSheet(OpenIGI.Core.Diagnostics.IOpenIgiLogger)
member.summary: Stacks the two streak strips into the one sheet the drops are drawn from.

remarks.para: The two images do not share a width — the defocused streaks are painted at twice the resolution, because a blurred shape needs the room a sharp one does not — so the narrower strip is expanded onto the wider one's grid by whole texels. Nearest, deliberately: an integer expansion of a sharp image is exact, and it is the render's own bilinear sampling that softens it back, whereas filtering here would blur the sharp strip twice.

Nothing bleeds across the seam. Both strips are painted with black margins at top and bottom — the streaks stop about a twentieth of the image short of each edge — so the rows either side of the join are empty in both, and a bilinear tap that straddles it picks up nothing. The mip chain would not cross it either — both strips are the same height, so the join sits at the halfway row of every level and no box in a halving chain straddles the middle of a power-of-two axis — but there is no chain, and that was measured rather than assumed.

Why the sheet is not mipped, having been. A streak is painted ten texels wide inside a fifty-texel cell and drawn across a handful of screen pixels, which is exactly the case mips exist for, and building one all but emptied the sky: a box filter spreads a thin bright line into its black surround and drops its peak in proportion, the vertex alpha then multiplies what is left, and the rain past twenty metres stopped being drawn at all. That is the physically honest answer to a sub-pixel streak and it is the wrong picture — the boost in exists precisely to stop distant rain falling under a pixel. Level zero it is, at the cost of some sparkle at range, which the temporal filter takes most of. If this is revisited, it needs a chain that preserves the streak's peak rather than its integral, not a plain box.

member.param: Told about a sheet that could not be read; the fallback is drawn instead.
member.returns: The sheet, and the v the defocused strip starts at.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Presentation.Rendering.PrecipitationSpriteSheets.TryLoadMask(System.String,OpenIGI.Core.Diagnostics.IOpenIgiLogger,OpenIGI.Core.Graphics.Bgra32[]@,System.Int32@,System.Int32@)
member.summary: Reads a greyscale mask and turns it into a white sprite whose alpha is the shape.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Presentation.Rendering.PrecipitationSpriteSheets.Stretch(System.ReadOnlySpan{OpenIGI.Core.Graphics.Bgra32},System.Int32,System.Int32,System.Span{OpenIGI.Core.Graphics.Bgra32},System.Int32,System.Int32)
member.summary: Copies one strip into the sheet, expanding it by whole texels to the sheet's width.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Presentation.Rendering.PrecipitationSpriteSheets.BuildFallbackSheet
member.summary: Generated streaks, for when the sheets are missing.

remarks.para: Kept because the alternative failure is silent and expensive: an asset that did not reach the output directory would otherwise mean no rain at all, which reads as a bug in the storm rather than as a missing file.

Drawn as what a falling drop looks like through a shutter, not as a line of paint. A drop is a lens: it is almost clear through the middle, and bright only along its two edges, where it bends the sky round into the eye and reflects it at a grazing angle -- so a streak is a thin tube with two bright rims and a faint body. The drop itself sits at the leading end as a small bead; behind it the smear thins out along the path it swept. Out of focus, near the lens, a drop spreads into a faint ring, which the defocused strip carries as a soft, hollow streak. Every cell varies the tube's weight and its rims, so one storm is not one repeated sprite.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Presentation.Rendering.PrecipitationSpriteSheets.UploadSheet(OpenIGI.Rendering.IGraphicsDevice,OpenIGI.Core.Graphics.Bgra32[],System.Int32,System.Int32,System.Int32)
member.summary: Uploads a sheet with as much of a mip chain as its cells can take.
member.param: Level zero.
Its width.
Its height.
The narrowest cell across the sheet, in texels.
member.returns: The texture.
member.remarks: A streak is a few texels of a painted line, and drawn a few pixels across without a chain it is sampled at scattered texels -- which broke every drop into a row of hard white dashes, rain as a dotted line of paint rather than water. The chain lets a small drop read as the soft, faint thing it is. It stops while a cell is still four texels wide, so the averaging never mixes one cell's streak into its neighbour's.

member.summary: How every one of the storm's sprite sheets is described to the device.
member.param: The sheet's width in texels.
Its height in texels.
member.returns: The description.

remarks.para: One mip level, and asking for none is not a way to ask for a chain. counts levels and requires at least one; zero makes level zero itself out of range, and the upload throws an before a texel is written. There is no mip generation behind this interface — a chain is uploaded level by level or it does not exist — so a sheet that wants one has to build it, not request it.

Asking for zero here took the WHOLE storm off the screen, not just the sheet that asked: the sprites are resolved together at the top of the draw, inside one try, and the splash sheet is resolved before the drops. One bad description and the curtains, the splashes and the rain all stopped being drawn at once.

remarks.para: The dome is turned so its axis points at the eye and scaled by its size over 2048 across, while its depth grows from nothing, (1 - remaining / life) * size + 0.01. Its texture is the model's animation (Mesh3D_SetAnimTextureFrame), stepped through once over its life.

The face group is transparent and additive, so it draws at ONE, ONE, unlit and unfogged (0x49EC70): the black around the flame adds nothing. Drawn alpha-blended instead, every card was an opaque square that the fog lightened into the box around the blast.

member.summary: Builds the FireBall's eye-facing, scaled orientation.
member.remarks: 0x480790 builds three rows -- across the view (-f.y, f.x, 0), then f x across, then the direction to the eye f, the dome's own axis -- and then takes their transpose as the model's frame, so in this engine's terms they are its columns. Used as rows, the dome's axis lay across the view and the flame showed edge on, a thin ring behind whatever exploded.

member.summary: How a title draws its .

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Presentation.Rendering.PrecipitationStyle.Igi1
member.summary: Project I.G.I.'s (Rain_FillVB, 0x499090): rain as a pixel-wide line rising from each drop, clear at its top and the weather's alpha at its foot; snow as a square of snow.tex facing the eye.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Presentation.Rendering.PrecipitationStyle.Igi2
member.summary: I.G.I. 2's (Rain_UpdateVertexBuffer): every drop a rectangle facing the eye in the weather's colour and alpha, rain three flakes wide and ten tall, drawn once for each of its density's scattered copies.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Presentation.Rendering.RetailPrecipitationRenderer
member.summary: Draws as both originals do: its one tile of drops repeated over the ground around the eye, in up to three layers above each tile, each stopping at the ground or roof beneath it.

remarks.para: Rain_UpdateGrid (0x498BD0) keeps a twelve-by-twelve ring of tiles about the eye, each holding the height a drop let fall from its corner would stop at -- the terrain or whatever stands on it, so the weather stops on a roof and never falls indoors. A tile that comes into the ring is dropped again; no more a frame than the eye moved tiles, all of them the first time.

Rain_Draw (0x498F10) and Rain_DrawCell (0x499430) draw the nine-by-nine tiles ahead of the ring's seam, farthest first, each with the quarter of the drops its tile's parity picks. The layers are 24576 units tall and stand on a floor that steps with the eye; a layer wholly above the tile's highest corner draws all its quarter, one below it none, and the layer it ends in only the drops still above it, which the quarter's list, highest first, makes a prefix.

The original's outcode test leaves out tiles wholly off one side of the screen; the device clips those anyway, so every tile whose four corners are known is drawn. Fog is off for it in both games; nothing it draws is far enough from the eye to fog.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Presentation.Rendering.ShadowCasterPass
member.summary: Draws the world into the sun's shadow cascades.

remarks.para: It draws through the same renderers the main pass uses, with a camera placed in the light instead of in the player's head. That is deliberate and is what the pass structure on exists for: a renderer asks for a mesh with a texture, and the device decides from the current pass that this one wants depth only. Neither presenter knows that shadows exist, and this pass does not know which game it is drawing.

The light camera sits at the player's position, not at the light. A directional light has no position, and the cascades are fitted in a frame whose origin is the camera — so putting the light camera anywhere else would mean every cascade matrix carrying a translation into single precision at level coordinates that run into the thousands. This is the same reason Camera3D.CreateModelView folds the camera offset into each object's transform.

Terrain casts through the caster the traced sun is given: the ground gathered from every direction around the eye, at the levels of detail the frame drew it with, rather than a descent from the light -- which would pick a tessellation for a viewpoint kilometres away. Without it a hill threw no shadow at all here, while the traced sun had it; the two shadow systems disagreed about the ground.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Presentation.Rendering.SkyCloudPlane
member.summary: How a scrolling cloud layer is sampled: one horizontal plane above the camera, faded by view depth.

remarks.para: Shared for the same reason the dome is. IGI.exe sub_51E1F0 and igi2ed's FlatSky_EnterHandler (0x653E10) compute the same three things per vertex: the point where the eye ray meets a plane Z Pos above the camera, a texture coordinate that is that point times the layer's scale plus the scroll, and a fade taken from the point's view depth. Even the constants match — the same 409.6 near cut-off, the same clamp at 0.999.

The plane is camera-relative in all three axes. I.G.I. 2 makes that unmistakable: the offset it feeds to the texture coordinate is the ray's, from the camera, never a world position. So a cloud layer does not slide past as the player walks and does not drop as the player climbs — the only thing that moves it is its own scroll. That is what makes it a sky rather than a ceiling.

How the original tessellates it, and why this does not. I.G.I. 2 builds a 26-vertex strip in screen space: it projects the horizon, fits an oriented box to the viewport around it, and walks thirteen rows across that box, unprojecting each vertex onto the plane only to obtain its texture coordinate and its fade. The construction exists to clip an unbounded plane to the viewport with a fixed-function pipeline. Re-emitting those unprojected points as world geometry is not equivalent — a row that crosses the true vanishing line unprojects to infinity, which costs the original nothing because it never uses the result as a position, and would throw geometry across the world here. A camera-centred polar grid is bounded by construction, is clipped by the hardware for free, and — because the surface is planar and the mapping affine — carries exactly the same texture across it.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Presentation.Rendering.SkyCloudPlane.NearCutoff

member.remarks: 409.60001 — a tenth of a metre. The same constant turns up in I.G.I. 2's sector renderer, so it reads as a shared near-plane figure rather than anything about the sky.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Presentation.Rendering.SkyDomeGeometry
member.summary: The sky dome's lattice and its shading, which both games build the same way.

remarks.para: This is one implementation because it is one piece of engine, not two that happen to look alike. Read side by side, IGI.exe sub_52CC40 and igi2ed SkyDome_InitialiseVertexBuffer (0x5717E0) lay out the same apex, the same fifteen rings of twenty, the same six- and eighteen-degree steps and the same skirt at half the radius below the horizon; sub_52CE90 and SkyDome_InterpolateVertexColour (0x5719B0) are the same two lerps and the same clamp.

Everything a title chooses is a parameter: the radius, the half angle, and six colours. I.G.I. 1 sizes the dome at 0.8 × its far plane; I.G.I. 2 fixes it at 8,000 units. Since the dome is a backdrop drawn with depth off, the radius sets nothing but the units the vertices are expressed in — which is exactly why it can differ between the titles without the geometry differing at all.

Lerp each band round the compass, lerp the two results down, then clamp each channel.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Presentation.Rendering.SkyRenderer
member.summary: Draws a level's sky: the gradient dome, then the scrolling cloud layers over it.

remarks.para: The sky is script data, not level geometry: a FlatSky task carries the dome colours, the fog colour and the cloud plane's shape, and each FlatSkyLayer child names a texture with a scale, a scroll speed, a tint and an alpha. Everything here is read from those tasks.

The dome follows the observed retail topology: an apex, fifteen rings six degrees apart, twenty vertices per ring, and a skirt half a radius below the horizon. The paired native listing confirms the 0.8 radius multiplier at 0x52CC40; the source of its base radius remains deliberately unnamed here until its renderer type is recovered. Colours run top → middle across [angle, 90°] and middle → bottom across [angle/2, angle]. It is drawn first, with no depth, centred on the camera.

A cloud layer is the plane Z Pos metres above the camera (sub_51E1F0): each vertex is textured by its camera-relative world position times the layer's scale plus the scroll, and faded by view depth — opaque nearer than d0 = D − (D − 0.1m) × fogAmount, then d0 × (1 − D/d) / (d0 − D) beyond it, clamped to [0, 0.999], where D is the task's Distance. The grid it is drawn on is the original's and is laid out across the SCREEN, not around the camera -- see , which is also where the two artefacts a camera-centred disc printed instead are written down. Divergence: the scroll's time base is the simulation tick assumed at 30 Hz; the original advances it per tick and the exact step has not been read.
Mission 1 declares no Lensflare task, so dome, clouds and the fog colour are everything its original sky draws. Levels that do declare one will need the flare ported.

member.summary: Vertices across each row of the strip, which the original spans in one quad.
member.remarks: Two is exact rather than coarse for an upright camera, which is what the game plays in. The texture coordinates are affine in the plane, so perspective interpolation across a quad reproduces them however wide it is; and the fade is by view depth, which along a screen line parallel to the horizon does not vary at all until the camera rolls. Rolled -- a cutscene, say -- the fade across a row becomes the linear approximation it is in the original too.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Presentation.Rendering.SkyRenderer.SetSunTint(OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3f)
member.summary: Tints the dome to the sun's warmth, rebuilding it when the tint moves enough to matter.
member.param: A per-channel multiplier, one for the authored sky, warmer as the sun sinks.
member.remarks: The dome's gradient is baked into its vertices, so a tint means rebuilding the mesh -- cheap for a dome of a few hundred vertices, but not worth doing every frame as the sun creeps. A small dead-band rebuilds only when the tint has shifted enough to see, so a still sun rebuilds once and a moving one a handful of times across the day.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Presentation.Rendering.SkyRenderer.TryBuildCloudGrid(OpenIGI.Core.Graphics.Camera3D@,OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Matrix4f@)
member.summary: Lays this frame's cloud strip across the screen and casts each of its vertices onto the plane, exactly as sub_51E1F0 does.
member.param: The camera the strip is laid out for.
The view-to-clip transform the strip is laid out in.
member.returns: when a strip was built; when the plane is not in front of the camera and nothing should be drawn.

remarks.para: The original builds this grid in screen space, and that detail is the whole of it. Two points on the plane -- the fade distance D ahead, and D to either side of that -- are projected, and the line through them is the strip's first row; twelve more rows step from there out to the edge of the viewport, each spanning the viewport's whole width. Every vertex is then the ray through its own screen position cast onto the plane, which is the same surface the plane always was, sampled where it is actually seen. Because the lateral axis is perpendicular to the view axis, that first row is parallel to the horizon whatever the camera does, and lies on the plane's side of it -- so no vertex can fall behind the camera, and the strip's outer edge sits exactly where the fade has reached zero.

The version before this drew a disc of 1.5 x D around the camera instead, and printed two artefacts for it. The disc has a rim, at atan(ZPos / 1.5D) above the horizon, with cloud on one side of it and bare sky on the other: missions 3 and 9 ask for ZPos 6 / D 40, which put that rim five and a half degrees up, and it was photographed there as a lens hanging in the sky. Every other mission asks for a plane 1.3 to 4 m up against 100 to 250 m of fade, which puts the same rim within a degree of the horizon. And the fade is by view depth, which runs to zero abreast of the camera and negative behind it, so the whole band of the disc level with the camera took the formula's "nearer than the fade starts" branch and came out at full opacity however far away it was. A screen-space strip has neither defect available to it: there is no rim on the screen to see, and every vertex is in front of the camera by construction.

remarks.para: Tiles are placed by their grid cell, at (column * tileWidth, row * tileHeight), which is how the original derives them — the positions stored alongside each cell are redundant. Empty cells are skipped.

Every tile edge is rounded to a whole pixel. Adjacent tiles share an edge, so rounding both sides of it the same way keeps them exactly adjacent; leaving them on fractional pixels instead makes each boundary a half-covered column that both neighbours blend into, which draws a visible grid over any picture whose left edge is not on an integer.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Presentation.Rendering.StatusMessageRenderer
member.summary: The remaster's presentation of the mission's status messages: a minimal comms feed at the top left when something happens, and the subtitle line that carries a spoken one.

remarks.para: The same messages, the same moments, a different surface. Timing, ordering and wrapping still come from the simulation — is what the original's slot array produces, typewriter and all — so this is a reskin in the strict sense: nothing here can make a message arrive earlier, hold longer, or appear in a different order than the retail path shows it in. StatusScreenRenderer.DrawStatusMessages is the faithful one; this is its counterpart, chosen by r_messages_tactical.

What is deliberately kept. The two-stage open is retail's own idea and a good one, so the card keeps it in spirit: it arrives by unfurling rather than by fading, and the text follows the panel rather than sharing its entrance. What changes is the execution — the original's opening flash is one 33 ms frame at three-quarters alpha, which on a modern display reads as a dropped frame rather than as emphasis, so here it becomes a short accent sweep along the card's leading edge.

What is deliberately dropped. The 235-pixel panel width and the 42-pixel step are authored against 640x480 and are far too tight for a card set in Barlow at a modern size, so this measures its own: the card is as wide as it needs to be up to a limit, and the column steps by the height each card actually took. A message that wraps to three lines therefore pushes the ones below it down instead of overlapping them, which the fixed step cannot do.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Presentation.Rendering.StormRenderer
member.summary: Simulates and draws the remastered storm: rain, the splashes it raises, and its far sheets.

remarks.para: The remastered counterpart to , which stays exactly as it is: that one is the original's rain, an analytic band of thin vertical streaks, and it is what the vanilla preset draws. This is a real particle system — drops are spawned, blown, aged and recycled, and each one knows where it is and how fast it is going.

Streaks alone look like the original, which is the whole point of the rest. A screen of thin grey lines is what the vanilla band already was; what reads as weather is everything around it — the ground answering with splashes, sheets of drizzle filling the distance past where individual drops stop resolving, and fat out-of-focus drops close to the lens that no amount of extra streaks substitutes for. All three are here, drawn from one vertex buffer as three contiguous ranges so the whole storm costs three draws.

The drops are images, not arithmetic. The streaks were procedural — a power curve across the quad, tapered at the ends — and a drop of falling water does not look like that. It is a wobbling, uneven line with beads of light strung along it where the surface catches. The sheet is two stacked strips of ten streaks each, the same ten sharp and defocused, and a drop keeps one index for its whole life and picks a strip by how far away it is. The shape of a streak inside its cell — its width, how much of the cell it fills lengthways, how much fatter the defocused one is — is named as a constant below.

Simulated on the CPU, deliberately. A storm of this shape is a couple of thousand live drops — spawn rate times lifetime — and at that count the simulation is microseconds. The frame this renderer lives in is GPU-bound, so the arithmetic is free where it is and would not be on the other side; what actually costs is the translucent overdraw, which is identical whoever moves the drops.

Where the ground is. Splashes need to know what a drop lands on, and this port has no cheap world height query — the ground query descends the octree per point, and a cast per drop is out of the question at these rates. is therefore a single plane, set each tick from the player's own feet. Within the dozen metres a splash is visible from, the ground under the player is what the rain is landing on; the approximation shows only on a steep slope or a rooftop below, and it costs nothing.

Not yet done here, and honest about it. Fading a drop out as it approaches a wall () needs the fragment shader to read scene depth, which no draw from this side can do; it is a backend change and is not attempted rather than faked. The same want blocks the drop's two brightest terms: ideally a drop would add a blurred, desaturated tap of the frame behind it — that is what backlighting and the ambient term stand for — and this pass cannot read the frame it is drawing into, so the sun's own colour and the level's ambient stand in for it. Wet surfaces and puddles are G-buffer work and live outside this file entirely.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Presentation.Rendering.StormRenderer.MaximumDrops
member.summary: The most drops ever alive, whatever the settings ask for.
member.remarks: This and the two below are one budget, not three: the whole storm is drawn from a single index buffer of , so their sum may never exceed 16,384 quads — one more and the fourth vertex of the last quad is index 65,536, which wraps to zero and folds the far end of the storm into a spray of triangles through the origin. There is deliberately a little room left under the ceiling.

member.summary: Draws one contiguous run of quads.
member.remarks: Additive, not alpha blended. Water does not take light out of what is behind it; it puts a little back, which is why rain reads against a dark wall as well as against a bright sky. Alpha blending with an ambient term that adds the frame behind the drop back on top very nearly cancels the attenuation the blend applied, and what is left is the lit drop, added. Alpha blended alone, every drop darkened whatever it crossed, and the storm sat over the scene like a sheet of scratched perspex.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Presentation.Rendering.SunGizmo
member.summary: A draggable, on-screen rotation gizmo for the sun, for the free camera.

remarks.para: Three world-axis rings float in front of the camera with a stub pointing at the current sun; dragging a ring turns the sun about that axis, exactly as the numpad keys of the do, but with the mouse. It is a screen-space gizmo: the rings are circles in world space, but they are projected to the screen through the same camera transform the frame is drawn with and then drawn and picked as flat polylines. That avoids a world-space line pipeline the renderer does not otherwise have, and picking a ring becomes a plain distance-to-polyline test against the cursor.

The drag maps the change in the cursor's angle about the gizmo's centre onto the ring's axis -- the motion any rotation gizmo answers to. It reads a freed cursor's absolute position, so the caller frees the cursor while the gizmo is up, the way the console does for its own pointer.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Presentation.Rendering.SurfaceHeights
member.summary: The height of whatever the rain would land on, sampled on a grid that follows the eye.

remarks.para: Why this exists. Rain should stop where it meets the world, so that it lands on roofs, steps, crates and the tops of walls. This port had one flat plane taken from the player's feet, so rain fell through every raised surface and every splash sat at one height. On a level of stacked concrete that is not a subtle difference: the ground floor rains and nothing else does.

Why a cache and not a ray per drop. A ray per drop per tick is thousands of traces a second through the object index, which is the reason the plane was there in the first place. But the answer a drop needs — how high is the world under this square metre — barely changes, and it is the same answer for every drop above that square. So the grid is sampled a few cells a tick, round-robin, and every drop reads it for free. A full sweep of the grid costs about as much as one drop's worth of tracing did, and it takes under a second, which is far quicker than the player can walk out of it.

It follows the eye in whole cells. Re-centring on a fractional position would shift every cached height sideways under the drops; snapping to the lattice means a step only ever scrolls whole cells in and out, and what scrolls in is marked unknown rather than being wrong.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Presentation.Rendering.TacticalComputerRenderer
member.summary: The remaster's map computer: a full-screen tactical interface drawn over a live overhead view of the level, set in the shell's own faces.

remarks.para: There is no device. The retail computer is a model held up in front of the camera with a 4:3 aperture cut in it, and everything the player came to read is inside that aperture — which at a modern resolution is a postage stamp in the middle of the screen surrounded by a low-polygon casing. This draws the map edge to edge and floats the interface over it, which is the whole reason the redesign exists. the retail map computer () keeps the original for the vanilla path; the two do not share code, because the one that must not change cannot be built out of the one that will.

The map is always underneath. Every page — the map, the objectives, the log — is drawn over the same live overhead pass, with the text pages laid on a translucent card rather than on a black rectangle. That is not decoration: it means switching pages never costs the player their sense of where they are, and it means the level is still moving behind the objective they are reading.

Everything is vector. The markers, the grid, the scale bar and the cursor are rectangles, triangles and text rather than sprites, so they are sharp at any resolution and can be coloured by meaning — hostile, complete, selected — instead of by which frame of which sprite happened to be authored. The one thing that would be worth a texture, the phosphor itself, is not drawn here at all: it is a display transform applied to the resolved scene, and this interface is drawn crisp on top of it, exactly as a real overlay on a real screen would be.

Fonts are owned here. The shell's faces are only built when the cinematic shell is, and the computer has to work under -vanillamenu too, so this loads its own through . The atlas cache on disk means that costs a file read rather than a rasterisation.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Presentation.Rendering.TextureDecodeCache
member.summary: Decodes a level's textures on worker threads, so the render thread only ever uploads them.

remarks.para: Turning a .tex into something uploadable is all CPU and none of it is graphics: the file is decoded, a cut-out is classified and its alpha widened, a mip chain is built by repeated box filters, and the chain's coverage is corrected against the alpha-test cutoff. Measured over a menu session it was the largest thing left on the render thread once the uploads stopped blocking — the mip chains alone, one texture at a time on the thread that also has to present.

None of it needs the device, and every texture is independent of every other, so it belongs where the rest of a backdrop is built: on a worker, ahead of the frame that wants it. The render thread's WorldTextureCache.GetTexture then finds the image already decoded and does nothing but create and upload.

The bytes are gathered once, here, before any worker starts. A registers what it reads from disk, so TryLoad writes to a plain dictionary and cannot be called from several threads at once. Reading on the building thread and handing the workers nothing but byte spans keeps every registry access on one thread, which is what makes this safe rather than merely fast.

Nothing here is load-bearing. A name the cache never saw, or one whose decode threw, simply is not in it, and the renderer decodes that one itself exactly as it always did. The cache is an optimisation with no semantics of its own.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Presentation.Rendering.TextureDecodeCache.AlphaTestCutoff
member.summary: The alpha below which a world texel is discarded rather than blended.
member.remarks: Lives here rather than on a renderer because two things have to agree on it: the draw that tests against it, and the decode that widens a cutout's alpha to survive it. The decode runs on a worker, ahead of any renderer existing, so the constant cannot belong to one.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Presentation.Rendering.TextureDecodeCache.MaxDecodeThreads
member.summary: How many cores the decode may take, leaving the rest to the thread drawing the frame.
member.remarks: Unbounded, this and the detail pack's own pass between them took every core the machine had, and the render thread was one of the things they took it from -- measured as a 600 ms frame on the level whose global-illumination convergence is heaviest, against 128 ms for the same frame when the decode was not running. Half the machine finishes the decode well inside the time the swap takes anyway, so the ceiling costs nothing and the frame keeps its cores.
