member.name: T:OpenIGI.Presentation.Rendering.TracerTrailRenderer
member.summary: Draws the ballistic rounds in flight: a glow at the head, a streak behind it, a fading ribbon tail.

remarks.para: The modern-shooter tracer, for the g_ballistics option. Each round is drawn as three things: a camera-facing glow dot at the interpolated head — the one part that survives being looked at end-on, which is exactly how the shooter sees their own round — a velocity-stretched head streak, and a trail ribbon through the round's recorded past positions, tapering and fading tailward. All are quads over one procedurally built glow texture, blended additively and never depth-written: a glow is light, and light does not occlude.

The texture carries its profile in the COLOUR channels with a solid alpha. The device blends src·srcA + dst with both texture and vertex colour multiplied in; putting the falloff in colour and alpha squares it and reads as nothing. Ribbons sample the texture's centre column (u = 0.5) so v runs across the radial profile's full brightness; only a streak's tip runs u out to the rim, which is what rounds it off.

The first metres of a player round are drawn from the gun, not the eye: the simulation flies the retail muzzle — the eye, dead centre of the screen, where a receding streak projects to a point — so each round carries a purely visual offset that converges onto the true trajectory over . The round every game since has drawn, for the same reason.

The colour is white, kept subtle, with only retail's gentle distance fade () applied — the retail amber-to-yellow ammunition gradient is available in but reads as flame against this game's dusk levels. Geometry is CAMERA-RELATIVE in double precision before narrowing, for the reason BulletMarkRenderer documents.

member.summary: The fraction of a tick's travel the head streak stretches over.
member.remarks: A round covers its whole inter-tick distance between two drawn frames, but stretching the quad over all of it reads as a solid rod. A third is the streak films actually leave on a sensor.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Presentation.Rendering.TracerTrailRenderer.MaximumQuads
member.summary: The most quads one frame may draw; anything past it is silently not drawn.
member.remarks: 2048 covers sixty-four rounds each trailing at full length. The cap exists because the mesh is FIXED-CAPACITY by design: it is created once and its vertices replaced in place each frame through — the same battle-tested path the CPU-skinned soldiers stream through every frame. The first cut destroyed and re-created a mesh per frame instead, and a buffer drawn on the very frame it was created is exactly the pattern that rasterised as a one-frame garbage quad — the intermittent black square — on a threaded driver.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Presentation.Rendering.ViewModelProjection
member.summary: Builds the first-person model's retail projection.
member.remarks: Retail's model renderer (0x49F700) copies the active transform context, selects layer zero, and installs it for the draw. The Direct3D setup at 0x493580 gives that layer a 204.8-unit near plane, half of the 409.6-unit world layer. With 4096 game units per metre that is 0.05 m. Keeping the model in this shallower foreground depth range preserves its own depth ordering. The foreground pass then resets its depth before drawing the rig, so close world geometry cannot occlude it.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Presentation.Rendering.ViewModelProjection.Create(System.Single,System.Single)
member.summary: Creates the first-person model projection for the supplied retail horizontal half-tangent.
member.remarks: Retail's 0x497D70 publishes independent pixel scales: the horizontal aperture is the supplied tangent and the vertical aperture is three quarters of it. This is deliberately not an aspect-correct world projection. Passing a 16:9 aspect ratio to widens a tan(30 degrees) foreground lens to about 75 degrees; retail keeps it at 60 degrees.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Presentation.Rendering.WorldCanvas
member.summary: A flat surface standing in the level, laid out in the same units an interface is, and drawn by projecting each quad's corners through the frame's own eye.

remarks.para: There is no third dimension in the sprite path, so a plane in the world is drawn by putting its corners where the camera says they are and letting the batch interpolate between them. What that buys over an overlay is everything perspective does — the surface shrinks as the player backs away from it, foreshortens as they look down on it, and slides across the object it belongs to as they walk past, because it is a thing in the level rather than a label about one.

It stands up and turns to the viewer. Its up is the world's, and its face is the horizontal direction back to the eye, so it is always square-on to read and never lies down or rolls with the camera. A surface pinned to the object's own facing would be more diegetic still and is a worse idea: half the things a player can use are approached from an angle the level author never set a facing for, and text seen at eighty degrees is not text.
Canvas coordinates are ordinary interface coordinates — x to the right, y downwards, origin at the anchor — so a layout written for the screen can be laid on the world unchanged.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Presentation.Rendering.WorldRenderer.MakeResident(OpenIGI.Game.World.WorldScene,System.Int32)
member.summary: Resolves one placement's mesh, textures and lightmap pages without drawing it.
member.param: The scene the placement belongs to.
Which placement to make resident.
member.returns: when named a placement.

remarks.para: Everything this renderer draws with is resolved the first time it is drawn and cached by name from then on: the geometry, the mesh upload, each texture, each lightmap page. That is the right behaviour for a level being walked through, where the cost is spread over the walk and nothing pays for a room it never enters. It is the wrong behaviour when the camera moves a long way in one frame — every model on the far side becomes visible at once, and the whole level's residency is paid for on a single frame.

The menu's backdrop makes that concrete: a slow orbit over one corner of the level leaves most of it unresolved, and pressing Play puts the camera at the player's spawn. Measured on mission 1, that one frame spent about 260 ms inside — not drawing, but uploading.

So this exists to pay that cost early and a little at a time, while the menu is idle. It resolves exactly what would resolve for the same placement and in the same order, which is the property that matters: anything it missed would simply be paid for later, on the frame that first drew it, and the point is that no frame pays.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Presentation.Rendering.WorldRenderer.Draw(OpenIGI.Game.World.WorldScene,OpenIGI.Core.Graphics.Camera3D@,OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Matrix4f@,System.Single,System.Boolean,System.Boolean,System.Boolean,System.Boolean,System.Boolean)

Skips placements whose model bounds are smaller than this radius in metres. Zero draws everything; the shadow pass raises it per cascade, because an object spanning a fraction of a texel of a far cascade cannot cast a shadow anyone reads.

Whether last frame's occlusion-query results may reject placements the frustum keeps. For the geometry pass only: indoors, the frustum still holds most of the level behind the walls, and these queries are what stop it being shaded. The shadow cascades must not pass this — their camera is the light's, and a query answered from the eye's depth says nothing about it.

Draws the translucent rotor attachments in place of the opaque world. The two are separate passes over the same placements: a rotor blends against what is already in the frame, so it has to follow every opaque draw and test depth without writing it. Its tallies accumulate onto the opaque pass's rather than replacing them, so the overlay still reads one frame.

Draws the level's glazing in place of the opaque world, over a picture the lighting has already finished. A SECOND pass over the same subsets rather than a diversion of them: a window texture holds the frame and the pane together, the opaque pass keeps the frame as it always did, and this keeps what that pass discarded. Like the rotors it tests depth without writing it, and its tallies accumulate onto the opaque pass's rather than replacing them.
Whether the pass is drawn from the frame's eye, so a placement the title's culling sees through a window is scissored to it (). A light's pass is never narrowed.
Draws only the face groups the original sorts and blends, over the opaque world.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Presentation.Rendering.WorldRenderer.IssueOcclusionQueries(OpenIGI.Core.Graphics.Camera3D@)
member.summary: Issues the queries the last occlusion-culled queued.
member.param: The same camera that pass drew from.
member.remarks: A separate step so the shell can call it once every opaque occluder of the frame — the world AND the terrain — is in the depth buffer. Issued inside the queries would miss whichever of the two draws after the world, and hills would stop hiding anything. Skipping the call costs nothing but culling: an unanswered query reports visible.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Presentation.Rendering.WorldRenderer.BuildDrawOrder(OpenIGI.Game.World.WorldScene)
member.summary: Orders the placements by render group, then by model so consecutive draws share GPU state.

remarks.para: The group has to be the outer key. The engine draws nothing directly: it enqueues each visible object into one of sixteen call queues by its group and empties them in order, so two objects in different groups are separated by everything the groups between them draw. Batching by model across that boundary would put a pane of glass before the wall behind it because the two happen to share a mesh name, which is the shape of every sorting complaint an I.G.I. 2 world can produce.
Model stays the inner key, so the state batching survives inside each group — which is where it was doing its work anyway, since a group is a run of objects rather than a scattering.

Project I.G.I. is unaffected to the bit. No shipped level of that game authors a group, so every placement carries , the first comparison is always nought, and the order is the one this produced before the key existed.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Presentation.Rendering.WorldRenderer.SubmitTracedOnly(OpenIGI.Game.World.WorldScene,OpenIGI.Presentation.Rendering.ResolvedWorldModel,OpenIGI.Game.World.WorldPlacement,OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Matrix4f@,System.Single,System.Single,System.Single,System.Single,System.Boolean)
member.summary: Offers a placement the camera will not draw to the traced world anyway.
member.param: The level, for resolving the model's subsets.
The model that was culled.
Its placement as displayed.
Where it stands, relative to the camera.
Its bounding sphere's centre in view space.
Its bounding sphere's centre in view space.
Its bounding sphere's centre in view space.
That sphere's radius, in metres.
Whether this pass is the one that feeds the traced world at all.

remarks.para: The bug this exists for. The acceleration structure was filled from the DRAW path, so it held exactly what the camera had at some point had in frame. A window reflects what is behind the camera, which by definition is the geometry the frustum just threw away — so a pane could only ever show a place the player had already stood and looked at. Measured at one window on mission one: 82 geometries and 587 placements in the structure facing the glass, against 150 and 1800 after sweeping the camera once across the yard behind it. The same window therefore reflected different things in two sessions, and more of the level the longer one played — which is not a tuning problem, it is the reflection being a function of where the player has looked.

The rule. Visibility decides what is DRAWN; the whole level is TRACED. Every placement is offered every frame whether the camera can see it or not, so the traced world holds the level's static geometry entire and keeps each placement exactly as long as it is still there.
Cheap: the backend's submission returns at once when there is no traced world, and for a placement it already holds the whole cost is a hash lookup per subset.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Presentation.Rendering.WorldRenderer.RotorCullBounds(OpenIGI.Core.Graphics.BoundingSphere@)
member.summary: Returns a rotor's bound across every phase and aerodynamic-tilt sample.
member.remarks: Rotor blur rotates the mesh around its local origin, so its usual off-origin bound centre moves over a circle. Centering the cull sphere at that origin and extending it by the centre's radius encloses every orientation without selecting a particular blade sample. That retains the full retail blur when visible and lets ordinary frustum culling reject a helicopter behind the camera.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Presentation.Rendering.WorldRenderer.ReloadTextures
member.summary: Drops every uploaded diffuse texture so the next draw loads them all again.

remarks.para: For swapping the upscaled pack in and out of a level that is already running, which is a comparison tool rather than a feature: the two pictures have to be the same frame, and a reload between them is the only way to be sure nothing else moved.

Clearing the dictionary is not enough, and that is the whole subtlety. A resolved model caches its subsets, and a WorldSubsetDraw carries its diffuse by value — so a texture dropped here would still be drawn from the cached draw list, by a handle that no longer exists. is the existing answer to exactly that, already used when the material library or the switchboard is replaced; the subsets re-resolve on next use at the cost of a dictionary lookup.

And the decode cache has to go with them. It holds images decoded on workers during the load, and prefers it over the archive — so leaving it would hand back the very pixels this is trying to replace. It is an optimisation with no semantics of its own, so dropping it costs a slower reload and nothing else.
Safe mid-frame: DestroyTexture queues the image and its descriptor sets for deletion once the frames that may still name them have cycled, rather than freeing under a frame in flight.

member.param: The level, for the placements that name which models are used.
How many texels per world unit a card asks for.
member.returns: What was captured, or when there was nothing to capture.

remarks.para: Here rather than in the shell because everything it needs is already here and private: the geometry cache, the uploaded meshes, the texture cache and the material library. Reaching in from outside would mean exposing all four, and the only caller wants none of them.

Once per distinct model, not per placement. A level draws the same crate hundreds of times and it looks the same every time. Spline-bent geometry is skipped entirely: it is unique to its placement, so it has no shared model whose cards could be reused, and cards for one-off geometry would be atlas spent on a single object.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Presentation.Rendering.WorldSubsetResolver.Dimmed(OpenIGI.Rendering.SurfaceMaterial,System.Single)
member.summary: The same surface with its lamp turned down, or turned off altogether.

remarks.para: Emission is not a brightness on this path — it is a SHADING MODEL. A surface with any emission at all is written to the G-buffer as unlit and comes out of the lighting pass as its own albedo times that number, so scaling it towards zero does not fade a panel back into the room: it fades it to black, and a switched-off lamp in a lit corridor ends up a hole in the wall.

So the last part of the fade is a handover rather than a ramp. Below the threshold the emission is dropped outright and the panel becomes an ordinary lit surface, which is what a dead fitting is. The threshold is low — under a third of albedo, dimmer than the same panel would be lit in any room worth lighting — so the step it costs is smaller than the step of leaving it out, and it lands two hundred milliseconds into a fade nobody is looking at the panel during.

It also has to clear , which is a quarter and is not a brightness at all: the G-buffer has no flags channel, so that one value in the emissive slot means "leave this surface out of the ambient occlusion". A lamp allowed to fade through it would spend a frame claiming to be that instead.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Presentation.Text.UiFontLibrary
member.summary: Loads the design's faces into GPU-resident s, cached to disk so the stb_truetype rasterisation is paid once.
member.remarks: The fonts ship in Assets/fonts under the OFL and are copied beside the executable by the desktop project. The atlas cache lives under the per-user data directory rather than the install folder, which may be read-only. Both the developer console and the R11 shell build their fonts through here so there is one place that knows where the faces are and at what size they are baked.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Presentation.Text.UiFontLibrary.Body
member.summary: The Barlow regular face used for body text.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Presentation.Text.UiFontLibrary.Emphasis
member.summary: The Barlow Condensed semibold face used for labels and letterspaced capitals.
member.remarks: The design sets every tab, button, value and HUD label in it, uppercase and tracked. The tactical computer sets nearly all of its chrome in it.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Presentation.Text.UiFontLibrary.Mono
member.summary: The JetBrains Mono regular face the developer tools are set in.

remarks.para: A monospaced face is not a style choice for the console, it is what makes it work. Every column in the variable browser and the log — value, default, flags, timestamp, category — can be placed on an integer multiple of one character advance measured once per size, instead of measuring every row's text on every frame. Numbers in a live watch list also stop shifting sideways as their digits change, which is the difference between reading a value and chasing it.
The same face the design uses for its eyebrows and key caps, so the developer tools read as part of the same product while keeping the fixed pitch their columns depend on.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Presentation.Text.UiFontLibrary.MonoMedium
member.summary: The JetBrains Mono medium face used for developer-tool headings.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Presentation.Text.UiFontLibrary.MonoBold
member.summary: The JetBrains Mono bold face used where a developer tool needs real emphasis.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Presentation.Text.UiFontLibrary.MonoPixelHeight
member.summary: The pixel height the developer tools' mono atlases are rasterised at.
member.remarks: The console draws at roughly 12–20 pixels, and a coverage atlas wants a source close to the sizes it is drawn at. The shell's 48 is far too large a source here: minifying it more than threefold thins the stems and the text greys out. Distance fields are the wrong tool for the same range — they soften exactly where a console needs to stay crisp.
